title: Why food spoils, and how drying, salt, sugar and cold keep it

summary.text: A jar of honey keeps for years on a shelf, but a bowl of cooked dal spoils in one day. Food spoils because microbes eat the food and multiply. Microbes are living beings too small to see. Microbes can grow only where there is free water, some warmth and food that is not too sour. Your child tests how much salt it takes to stop dal water from spoiling. They also find that thin jaggery water ferments while thick jaggery syrup keeps. They learn how drying, salt, sugar, sourness, oil, cold and heat each take away something microbes need. They see how families across India use these methods. They also meet the helpful microbes that guard curd and pickle, and the ones that live in the gut.
summary.art: A kitchen shelf with a jar of honey, a jar of mango pickle under oil and a tin of papad, beside a bowl of dal with froth on top.

intro.hook: A jar of honey can sit on a shelf for years and never spoil. A bowl of cooked dal spoils in one day. Both are wet. So why does one keep and the other spoil?
intro.text: Food spoils because microbes eat the food before we do. Microbes are living beings too small to see, such as bacteria, yeasts and moulds. They are in the air, on our hands and on every food. They grow fast in cooked dal, because dal gives them food, water and warmth. In this unit you find out what stops them. You set up five glasses of dal water with more and more salt in each, which we call the Salt Ladder. You keep thin jaggery water beside thick jaggery syrup. You dry tomato slices and weigh the water that leaves. By the end you can explain why honey keeps. You can also explain why a wet spoon must never go into the pickle.
intro.art: A jar of golden honey and a steel bowl of cooked dal side by side on a kitchen counter, with a calendar on the wall behind them.

outcomes: By the end I can explain that microbes spoil food, and say what bacteria, yeasts and moulds need to grow.
By the end I can explain how drying, salt, sugar, sourness, oil, cold and heat each keep food.
By the end I can use my own test results to explain why the amount of salt or sugar matters.
By the end I can tell spoiled food from fermented food, and from changes that microbes do not cause.
By the end I can say what helpful microbes do in curd, in my gut and in the soil.
By the end I can plan a fair test with a ladder of amounts, and chart the results.
By the end I can say what scientists still argue about, such as fermented foods and gut microbes.

terms.meaning: A living being too small to see without a microscope. Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are microbes.
terms.example: One spot of mould on bread is many thousands of microbes living together.
terms.art: A slice of bread with one green spot, and a circle zooming in to show many tiny threads and round spores.

terms.meaning: Microbes made of one very small cell each. One alone is called a bacterium. In warm, wet food some bacteria can split in two every 20 to 30 minutes.
terms.example: Bacteria turn milk into curd. Other bacteria turn cooked dal frothy and sour on a warm counter.
terms.art: A bowl of dal with froth on top, and a circle zooming in to show many small rod-shaped cells, some splitting in two.

terms.meaning: A fungus who grows as fine threads and makes fuzzy patches on food. Moulds need air, and they can grow on food that is too dry for most bacteria.
terms.example: The green and white fuzz on old bread, on a forgotten lemon or on top of a pickle is mould.
terms.art: A lemon half covered in blue-green fuzz, with fine threads drawn reaching down into the fruit.

terms.meaning: A fungus who lives as single round cells. Yeasts eat sugar and give off carbon dioxide gas and a little alcohol.
terms.example: Yeasts make bread rise. Wild yeasts also make jaggery water and fruit juice bubble when they are left out.
terms.art: A glass of brown jaggery water with small bubbles rising, and a circle zooming in to show round yeast cells with small buds.

terms.meaning: A tiny, tough cell that moulds and some bacteria make. A spore can wait, dry, for months or years, and grows when water and food are there.
terms.example: Mould spores float in the air of every room. They land on a papad and wait. If the papad gets damp, they grow.
terms.art: A papad with tiny dots landing on it from the air, and a second damp papad where the dots have grown into fuzzy patches.

terms.meaning: The change in food when unwanted microbes grow there. The smell, taste, colour or feel changes, and the food may become unsafe.
terms.example: Milk that smells sour and splits, bread with green spots and slimy spinach are all spoiled.
terms.art: Three foods on a plate: a split glass of milk, a slice of bread with green spots and a bunch of dark slimy leaves.

terms.meaning: Keeping food safe to eat for longer, by stopping the growth of microbes.
terms.example: Drying fish, salting mango, making jam and keeping milk in the fridge are all ways of preserving food.
terms.art: A row of preserved foods: dried fish on a string, a pickle jar, a jam jar and a milk packet in an open fridge.

terms.meaning: Water in a food that microbes are able to take in. Water that salt or sugar is holding is not free. Scientists call the measure of free water 'water activity'.
terms.example: Honey is about one-sixth water, but sugar holds nearly all of that water. So honey has very little free water, and microbes do not grow in honey.
terms.art: A drop of honey zoomed in to show small water particles each surrounded and held by larger sugar particles.

terms.meaning: Taking the water out of something. Dehydrated food is dried food.
terms.example: Red chillies spread in the sun in Guntur lose their water in a few days. The dry chillies keep for a year.
terms.art: A wide mat covered in red chillies drying in bright sun, with wavy lines of water vapour rising.

terms.meaning: Water with a lot of salt dissolved in it. Brine for pickling holds 10 grams of salt or more in every 100 millilitres.
terms.example: In Kerala, small green mangoes are kept for months in a jar of brine. This pickle is called uppu manga.
terms.art: A tall ceramic jar filled with small green mangoes under cloudy salt water.

terms.meaning: The movement of water through the thin skin of a cell. The water moves towards the side with more salt or sugar dissolved.
terms.example: A microbe who lands in thick sugar syrup loses water through their cell skin by osmosis. They shrink and stop growing.
terms.art: A round cell in plain water looking plump, and the same cell in syrup looking shrunken, with small arrows showing water leaving.

terms.meaning: A substance that tastes sour. Lemon juice, tamarind, vinegar and curd all hold acids. Most microbes that spoil food grow poorly in strong acid.
terms.example: Tamarind rice keeps on a train journey for a day or more, partly because tamarind makes the rice sour.
terms.art: A lemon, a ball of tamarind, a bottle of vinegar and a bowl of curd on a table.

terms.meaning: A change that chosen microbes make in food as they eat sugar. They leave behind acid, gas or alcohol. The acid also helps to keep the food.
terms.example: Bacteria ferment milk into curd. The acid they make gives curd a sour taste and holds back other microbes.
terms.art: A bowl of milk turning into set curd, with tiny bacteria drawn and small arrows labelled acid.

terms.meaning: Heating a food enough to kill most microbes, followed by fast cooling. Milk is heated to 72 degrees Celsius for 15 seconds.
terms.example: A milk packet says 'pasteurised'. The milk still has a few microbes, so the packet must stay in the fridge.
terms.art: A milk packet with the word pasteurised on it, beside a small drawing of milk flowing through a hot pipe and then a cold pipe.

terms.meaning: Closed so well that air and water vapour cannot get in or out.
terms.example: Biscuits stay crisp in an airtight dabba. In an open plate they take in water from the air and go soft.
terms.art: A steel dabba with a tight lid holding crisp biscuits, beside an open plate with a bent, soft biscuit.

terms.meaning: Any one thing that makes a food harder for microbes to grow in. Preserved foods often use several small hurdles together.
terms.example: Mango pickle uses four hurdles: a lot of salt, sour mango, mustard and a layer of oil that keeps air out.
terms.art: A cartoon running track with four low hurdles labelled salt, sour, spice and oil, and small microbes stopping at each.

terms.meaning: A substance added to food in a small, measured amount to slow microbes. A label lists each one by name or number.
terms.example: A squash bottle may list 'preservative (211)'. That number means sodium benzoate.
terms.art: A hand holding a bottle of orange squash, with the ingredients list enlarged and one line circled.

terms.meaning: A poison made by a living being. Some bacteria and moulds leave toxins in food, and some of these toxins stay even after the food is boiled.
terms.example: Rice left out all day can hold a toxin from bacteria. Heating the rice again kills the bacteria but may not remove the toxin.
terms.art: A pot of rice on a stove with steam rising, and a small warning sign beside it.

terms.meaning: The bacteria and other microbes who live in your intestines. There are tens of trillions of them. They eat the parts of plants that you are unable to digest.
terms.example: When you eat dal, vegetables and fruit, your gut microbes ferment the fibre. They make substances that feed the cells of your gut wall.
terms.art: An outline of a child's belly with the large intestine drawn, and a circle zooming in to show many kinds of bacteria around bits of plant fibre.

explanations.concept: Why food spoils: microbes eat the food before we do
explanations.definition: Food spoils when bacteria, yeasts or moulds grow in the food. They eat the food, multiply, and leave behind acids, gases and other substances that change the smell, taste and look.
explanations.description: Microbes are everywhere. Mould spores float in the air, bacteria live on hands, spoons and vegetable skins, and wild yeasts sit on fruit. So every food already carries some. They feed by breaking the big molecules of the food, such as starch and protein, into small ones. They take the energy and let the leftovers go. Those leftovers are what we notice. Acids taste sour. Gases make froth and bubbles. Some small molecules smell very bad, such as the ones from spoiled fish or eggs. Bacteria multiply by splitting in two. In warm, wet food some kinds can split every 20 to 30 minutes. So a few bacteria can become millions in a few hours. This is why cooked dal that was fine at lunch can be spoiled by the next morning.
examples: Cooked dal left on the counter overnight in summer turns frothy and sour. Bacteria have multiplied in the dal.
A lemon forgotten in a basket grows blue-green mould. The mould's threads spread through the fruit as they feed.
Sweet palm sap, called neera, starts to ferment within a few hours in warm air. Wild yeasts eat the sugar. Kamala Sohonie, the first Indian woman to earn a PhD in science, studied neera as a food.
explanations.art: A bowl of dal drawn three times, at lunch, at night and the next morning, with a few dots, then many dots, then froth.

explanations.definition: Microbes that spoil food need five things: food, free water, enough warmth, enough time, and food that is not too sour. Moulds also need air.
explanations.description: Take away any one of these and growth slows or stops. Most spoiling bacteria grow fastest between about 20 and 45 degrees Celsius, which is the warmth of an Indian kitchen. They grow slowly in a fridge at about 4 degrees, and stop in a freezer. They need water they can take in. So they grow in dal, milk, cooked rice and cut fruit, but not in dry rice or atta. Most stop in very sour food. Moulds are tougher in two ways: they grow on drier and more sour food than most bacteria. But moulds must have air. Some bacteria are the opposite, and grow only where there is no air at all. So no single method stops every microbe, and that is why many foods use more than one method.
examples: Raw rice keeps for a year. Cook the same rice, which adds water, and the rice spoils in a day.
Bread in a closed plastic bag grows mould within a week in the monsoon. The bag holds the dampness in.
Milk in the fridge keeps for days. The same milk on a summer counter can spoil within a day.
explanations.art: Five small pictures in a row labelled food, free water, warmth, time and not too sour, with a sixth labelled air beside a patch of mould.

explanations.concept: Free water: why honey is too dry for microbes
explanations.definition: Microbes can use only free water, which is water that nothing else is holding. Salt and sugar hold on to water. So a very salty or very sweet food can feel wet and still have too little free water for microbes.
explanations.description: A microbe is a cell with a thin skin, and water passes through that skin. Water moves towards the side with more salt or sugar dissolved in it. This movement is called osmosis. In thick syrup or strong brine, the water inside the microbe moves out. The cell shrinks and stops growing. Scientists measure free water on a scale from 0 to 1, called water activity. Pure water is 1. Fresh bread is about 0.95, jam about 0.8 and honey about 0.6. Most bacteria stop growing below about 0.9, and most moulds below about 0.8. Almost nothing grows below 0.6. Honey is about one-sixth water, and bread is more than one-third water. But in honey the sugar holds the water, and in bread much of the water is free. So bread grows mould and honey keeps.
examples: In the Thick or Thin experiment, thin jaggery water ferments within a few days. Thick jaggery syrup usually stays unchanged.
Jam is about two-thirds sugar. An opened jar still keeps for weeks.
Honey mixed with water can ferment, because yeasts now have free water. People have made a drink from honey and water this way for thousands of years.
explanations.art: A scale from 0 to 1 drawn like a ruler, with dry biscuit, honey, jam, bread and water placed along it, and marks where moulds and bacteria stop.

explanations.definition: Drying removes most of the water from a food. With too little free water, microbes on the food stop growing. They are not killed. Many wait as spores, and grow again if the food gets damp.
explanations.description: Sun and moving air carry water away from thin pieces of food. A tomato is about 94 parts water in every 100, so a dried tomato slice weighs very little. Dried food must then be kept dry. Dry food takes in water from damp air. That is why papad in an open tin goes soft and mouldy in the monsoon. Families dry food in the hot, dry months for this reason. Ghee is a dried food too. Butter is about one-sixth water. When butter is heated, the water boils away as bubbles, and the milk solids are strained out. What is left is almost pure fat with almost no water, so ghee keeps for months without a fridge. Freeze-drying is a modern way of drying. The food is frozen, and the ice is drawn off as vapour, so the food keeps its shape.
examples: Vadam and vathal are dried on terraces in Tamil Nadu in March and April, before the rains.
Salted fish dries on racks along the coasts of Kerala, Konkan and Odisha.
In Kashmir, brinjal, gourd and tomato are dried on strings in autumn. They are cooked in winter, when snow closes the roads.
Milk powder, instant coffee and the food astronauts carry are dried in factories.
explanations.art: A terrace in bright sun with rows of white vadam on a cloth, a string of dried brinjal slices and a rack of drying fish.

explanations.concept: Salt and sugar: the amount matters
explanations.definition: Salt and sugar preserve food only in large amounts. A little salt or sugar does not stop microbes, and a little sugar feeds them.
explanations.description: The salt we add for taste is about 1 gram in 100 grams of food. That is far too little to hold back microbes. Sea water has about 3.5 grams of salt in 100 millilitres, and many bacteria live in the sea. Pickling brine has 10 to 20 grams in 100 millilitres. Sugar works the same way. A spoon of sugar in a glass of water is food for yeast. Jam and murabba are more than half sugar, and at that strength the sugar holds the water. This is why pickle is very salty and jam is very sweet. They could not keep otherwise. It is also why we eat them in small amounts. Too much salt or sugar is not good for the body.
examples: In the Salt Ladder experiment, the glasses with no salt and a quarter teaspoon of salt usually spoil first. The glasses with 2 and 4 teaspoons usually stay clear.
Amla murabba from Uttar Pradesh keeps for a year in thick sugar syrup.
Lemon pickle in salt needs about one part salt to five or six parts lemon by weight.
explanations.art: Five glasses in a row with more and more salt marked on their labels, the first two cloudy and frothy and the last two clear.

explanations.concept: Sourness and fermentation: helpful microbes guard the food
explanations.definition: Most microbes that spoil food or make people ill grow poorly in strong acid. We can add an acid, such as vinegar, lemon or tamarind. Or we can let helpful bacteria make the acid, which is fermentation.
explanations.description: When a spoon of curd goes into warm milk, the curd bacteria multiply fast. They eat the milk sugar and make lactic acid. The acid sets the milk and makes it sour. Now the curd is a poor place for most other microbes. So curd keeps longer than the milk it came from. The curd bacteria were there first. They used up the milk sugar and made the milk too sour for most other microbes to grow. The same thing happens in idli batter and in gajar kanji from North India. It also happens in gundruk, the fermented leafy greens of Sikkim and Nepal. Fermenting keeps food by choosing which microbes grow there. Some of these bacteria also make substances that harm other bacteria. One of them, nisin, is now used as a food preservative.
examples: Curd keeps for a few days in the fridge, and pasteurised milk from an opened packet for about two.
Puliyodarai, tamarind rice, is packed for long journeys in Tamil Nadu and Karnataka. The tamarind and oil help the rice keep.
Vinegar onions and kasundi, the mustard sauce of Bengal, are kept by their sourness.
explanations.art: A bowl of curd zoomed in to show many curd bacteria filling the space, with a few other microbes outside unable to enter.

explanations.definition: Cold slows microbes down but does not kill them. Strong heat kills them. Sealing a food after heating stops new microbes from getting in.
explanations.description: In a fridge at about 4 degrees Celsius, most bacteria split only once in many hours, so food lasts days. In a freezer at minus 18 degrees there is no liquid water and growth stops. When the food warms up, the microbes who lived through the cold grow again. Boiling kills most microbes, but the spores of some bacteria live through boiling. Pasteurised milk is heated to 72 degrees for 15 seconds, which kills most microbes and leaves the taste. Some milk is sold in cartons that keep for months without a fridge. That milk has been heated to about 140 degrees for a few seconds and packed with no microbes. Tinned food is sealed and then heated to about 121 degrees. That heat is needed because one kind of bacterium grows without air and makes a deadly toxin. A tin or packet that has swollen has gas made by microbes inside, and must be thrown away unopened. In the early 1900s the American chemist Mary Engle Pennington studied eggs, milk and chicken on the way to shops. She worked out how cold they must be kept. She also led a study of cold railway wagons for carrying food.
examples: An unopened carton of long-life milk keeps for months on a shelf. Once opened, it needs the fridge like any milk.
Apples from Himachal Pradesh are kept in cold stores, so they can be sold many months after the harvest.
Frozen peas keep for a year, and cook like fresh ones.
explanations.art: A thermometer drawn tall, marked at minus 18, 4, 30, 72 and 121 degrees, with small pictures of a freezer, a fridge, a kitchen counter, a milk pipe and a tin.

explanations.definition: A hurdle is anything that makes a food harder for microbes to grow in. Many preserved foods use several hurdles at once, even though each one on its own would be too weak to keep the food safe.
explanations.description: The German food scientist Lothar Leistner gave this idea its name. A microbe who can get past one hurdle is often stopped by the next. Mango pickle is a good example. The salt holds the water. The raw mango is sour. Mustard and chilli slow some microbes. The layer of oil on top keeps air away from moulds. If one hurdle fails, the others may still hold. But a wet spoon brings in fresh water. As the oil is used up, pieces of mango stick out above it, and mould can start there. A food label often tells you about its hurdles. When a label says 'Refrigerate after opening', it means that the sealed jar was keeping microbes out. Once you break the seal, that hurdle is gone, so the cold of the fridge has to do the job instead.
examples: Tomato ketchup uses vinegar, sugar, salt, heating and a sealed bottle.
Dried fish is both salted and dried.
Smoked meat and fish in Nagaland hang above the kitchen fire. They are dried by the heat, and the smoke leaves substances that slow microbes.
explanations.art: A jar of mango pickle with four arrows pointing to it, labelled salt, sour mango, mustard and chilli, and oil on top.

explanations.definition: Not every change in food is spoiling. Fermenting is a change made by microbes that we chose. Some other changes are not made by microbes at all.
explanations.description: A cut apple turns brown within 20 minutes. Substances in the apple react with oxygen from the air. No microbe is needed, and the apple is safe. A banana skin turns black as the banana ripens, which is the fruit's own work. Old fried snacks smell like paint because oxygen has changed the oil. This is called going rancid. A biscuit that bends has taken in water from the air. Honey that turns grainy has only formed sugar crystals. A potato that grows shoots is alive and growing. To tell these apart, ask three questions. Did someone add a starter or set this food to ferment on purpose? Is there fuzz, slime, froth or a bad smell that was not there before? Could air or water alone have done this? When food that was not meant to ferment is frothy, slimy, fuzzy or foul-smelling, throw it away.
examples: Idli batter that has risen and smells pleasantly sour is fermented. Dal that has frothed and smells sharp is spoiled.
Milk that splits when lemon juice is added has been curdled by acid. This is how paneer is made.
At the market, fresh fish has clear eyes and a firm body, and fresh leaves are crisp and not slimy.
explanations.art: Three plates labelled spoiled, fermented and only changed, holding mouldy bread, a bowl of risen batter and a brown cut apple.

explanations.concept: Food that looks fine can still be unsafe
explanations.definition: Spoiled food usually warns us with smell or looks. But some microbes that make people ill do not change the food in a way we can notice.
explanations.description: The microbes that make food smell bad are often not the ones that make people ill. Some harmful bacteria can reach dangerous numbers while the food still looks and smells normal. Some leave toxins that boiling does not destroy. Moulds send fine threads deep into soft food, far beyond the fuzzy patch, and some moulds make toxins. So cutting the mould off bread, fruit or cooked food does not make the food safe. A few simple rules follow from the science. Eat cooked food within about two hours, or put it in the fridge. Heat food from the fridge until it is steaming. Keep raw meat, fish and eggs away from food that will not be cooked. If spoiled food is eaten by mistake, it can cause vomiting, loose motions and stomach pain. The body loses water, so the person should sip ORS or water. See a doctor if it lasts more than a day, or at once for a small child.
examples: Cooked rice kept warm all day can cause vomiting even after it is fried again.
Groundnuts and maize stored damp can grow a mould whose toxin harms the liver. This is one reason farmers dry their grain well.
Unsafe food makes about 600 million people ill every year, by the World Health Organization's count.
explanations.art: A plate of rice that looks perfectly fresh, with a magnifying circle showing many bacteria that the eye is unable to see.

explanations.definition: Tens of trillions of bacteria live in your large intestine. They digest parts of food that you are unable to digest, and they make some vitamins. They also take up space that harmful microbes would otherwise use.
explanations.description: Your own enzymes are unable to break down most plant fibre. Your gut microbes ferment the fibre. As they do, they make small molecules that feed the cells of your gut wall. They also make vitamin K and some B vitamins. A person carries about as many bacteria as they have cells of their own. A gut with many kinds of microbes is usually a sign of good health. One large study looked at more than 10,000 people. Those who ate 30 or more kinds of plants in a week had more kinds of gut microbes. Those who ate fewer than 10 kinds had fewer. After an upset stomach or a course of antibiotics, the gut microbes take time to return to their usual numbers.
examples: A meal of rice, sambar and a vegetable poriyal can hold eight or more kinds of plants.
Babies are born with almost no gut microbes. They collect them from their mother, from milk and from the world around them.
Outside the body, soil bacteria and fungi do the same work on fallen leaves and peels. They turn them into food for plants.
explanations.art: An outline of a child with the large intestine shown, many colours of bacteria drawn inside, and small arrows from bits of vegetable to the bacteria and from the bacteria to the gut wall.

explanations.concept: Do fermented foods and probiotics change your gut microbes?
explanations.definition: Curd, buttermilk, kanji and other fermented foods hold living bacteria. Scientists agree these foods are safe and nourishing. They disagree about whether the bacteria in them settle in the gut and change a person's health.
explanations.description: More than a hundred years ago, the scientist Elie Metchnikoff suggested that bacteria in sour milk help people live longer. Today shops sell probiotic drinks and capsules with the same promise. The tests so far give mixed answers, and what holds for one person may not hold for another.
examples: Many families give curd rice or buttermilk after an upset stomach.
Probiotic drinks are sold with claims about digestion and immunity.

perspectives.who: Scientists at Stanford University, in a study published in 2021
perspectives.explanation: They asked 36 healthy adults to eat either more fermented foods or more fibre for ten weeks. The people who ate more fermented foods ended with more kinds of gut microbes. They also had lower signs of inflammation in their blood.

perspectives.who: Scientists at the Weizmann Institute in Israel, in a study published in 2018
perspectives.explanation: They gave people probiotic bacteria and then looked inside the gut. In some people the new bacteria settled. In others they passed straight through. So a probiotic may do something for one person and nothing for another.

Fermented foods are good foods, and eating them is sensible. But most studies are small and short. No one should expect curd or a probiotic drink to cure an illness. A healthy child does not need costly capsules.

explanations.art: A bowl of curd and a small bottle of probiotic drink on a table, with a question mark drawn over an outline of a belly.

explanations.definition: Every region of India has its own preserved foods. Each one fits the local weather, the local crops and the months when fresh food is hard to get.
explanations.description: People preserve food when there is plenty, to eat when there is little. Mangoes come only in summer, so they are pickled, dried or cooked in sugar. Fish are plentiful after the monsoon, so they are salted and dried. In the Himalayas, snow closes roads for months, so vegetables and cheese are dried in autumn. The method fits the weather. Hot, dry places dry their food in the sun. Wet places, such as the Northeast, use smoke and fermentation, because food does not dry well in damp air. These methods were worked out over hundreds of years, mostly by women, long before anyone had seen a microbe. People tested, watched what kept and what spoiled, and passed on the rules.
examples: South: avakaya in Andhra Pradesh and Telangana, vathal in Tamil Nadu, sandige in Karnataka, dried fish and uppu manga in Kerala.
West: chhundo in Gujarat, kokum in Konkan and Goa, ker sangri in Rajasthan.
North: amla murabba in Uttar Pradesh, wadiyan in Punjab, dried vegetables in Kashmir, hard dried cheese called chhurpi in Ladakh.
East and Northeast: badi in Odisha, kasundi in West Bengal, gundruk in Sikkim, fermented bamboo shoot in Manipur, smoked meat in Nagaland.
explanations.art: A simple outline map of India with small pictures placed on it: a pickle jar in Andhra Pradesh, drying fish in Kerala, a string of dried vegetables in Kashmir and a smoking rack in Nagaland.

explanations.concept: The same rules keep a mummy, a mammoth and an astronaut's dinner
explanations.definition: The things that keep food also keep anything else that microbes would eat. Dryness, salt, sugar and cold have preserved bodies, seeds and food for thousands of years.
explanations.description: In ancient Egypt, bodies were packed in a natural salt called natron for about 40 days. The salt drew out the water, and the dried bodies have lasted for thousands of years. Honey was also left in Egyptian tombs, and sealed honey is known to keep for a very long time. In Siberia, frozen ground has kept woolly mammoths, with hair and flesh, for tens of thousands of years. A man died in the Alps about 5,300 years ago. He was found in the ice in 1991, with his last meal still in his stomach. On an island near the North Pole, a vault holds dried seeds from all over the world. The vault is kept at minus 18 degrees Celsius. Astronauts eat food that has been dried or heated and sealed. The Defence Food Research Laboratory in Mysuru has prepared packed foods such as idli and upma for India's astronauts. Nobody yet knows how to keep a full, tasty diet fresh for a journey to Mars that could last years.
examples: Egyptian mummies were dried with salt.
Frozen mammoths were kept by cold.
Space food is dried, or heated and sealed.
explanations.art: Three panels: an Egyptian jar of honey, a mammoth tusk sticking out of frozen ground, and an astronaut holding a sealed food pouch.

agreed.text: Food spoils because microbes grow in the food. Air alone does not spoil food.
agreed.evidence: In the 1860s Louis Pasteur kept boiled broth open to the air in flasks with long bent necks. The necks trapped dust and microbes. The broth stayed clear. Tinned food that was not heated enough spoils even though no air is inside.

agreed.text: Microbes need free water to grow, and salt and sugar take free water away.
agreed.evidence: In the 1950s an Australian scientist, William James Scott, measured how microbes grow in foods. Their growth followed the free water, and not the total amount of water. Food scientists have used his measure ever since.

agreed.text: Cold slows the growth of microbes but does not kill most of them.
agreed.evidence: Food taken out of a freezer and left warm spoils as fast as fresh food. Bacteria have been grown from food kept frozen for years.

agreed.text: Heating food in a sealed container preserves the food, if the heat is strong enough to kill spores.
agreed.evidence: Nicolas Appert showed this with bottles in 1810. In the 1890s Samuel Prescott and William Underwood found living bacteria in swollen tins that had been heated too little. They worked out the heating times that prevent this.

agreed.text: The acid made by fermenting bacteria holds back most other microbes.
agreed.evidence: Curd, pickled vegetables and fermented batters have been measured in many laboratories. As the acid rises, the numbers of other bacteria fall.

agreed.text: About as many bacteria live in and on a person as the person has cells of their own.
agreed.evidence: In 2016 Ron Sender, Shai Fuchs and Ron Milo counted again with better data. They found about 38 trillion bacteria and about 30 trillion human cells in an adult. Older books said ten times as many bacteria, which was wrong.

challenging.claim: Air spoils food, so food keeps if all the air is removed.
challenging.who: The French chemist Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac, in 1810, and many scientists for years after
challenging.for: Food sealed in bottles and heated did keep. When the bottles were opened to the air, the food spoiled.
challenging.against: Pasteur showed that microbes carried in the air do the spoiling. Some bacteria grow best with no air at all, and they spoil tins that were heated too little.
challenging.context: This card is about an old explanation of why sealed, heated food keeps.

challenging.claim: If you cut the mould off, the rest of the food is fine.
challenging.for: The fuzzy patch is the only part that looks or smells bad, and the rest tastes normal.
challenging.against: The fuzz is only the part of the mould that makes spores. Fine threads run deep into soft foods such as bread, fruit and cooked food, and some moulds leave toxins there. Food safety agencies say to throw such food away.
challenging.context: This card is about what to do with food that has a spot of mould.

challenging.claim: A fridge kills microbes, so food in the fridge is safe for as long as you like.
challenging.for: Food in the fridge lasts far longer than food on the counter.
challenging.against: Cold only slows microbes. A few kinds keep growing slowly at fridge temperature. Cooked food in a fridge is best eaten within two or three days.
challenging.context: This card is about what a fridge really does to microbes.

challenging.claim: Food with added preservatives is harmful, and food without them is always better.
challenging.for: Some people react badly to certain preservatives. Food made fresh at home needs none.
challenging.against: Preservatives are allowed only in small, tested amounts, and they prevent food poisoning and waste. Salt and sugar are preservatives too, and eating a lot of them harms health more surely. The fair question is how much of each, not whether a label has a number.
challenging.context: This card is about the preservatives listed on food labels.

challenging.claim: People in hot countries use more spices because spices stop food from spoiling.
challenging.who: Jennifer Billing and Paul Sherman, two American biologists, in 1998
challenging.for: They studied thousands of recipes from 36 countries. Hotter countries used more spices, and many spices slow bacteria in laboratory tests.
challenging.against: In 2021 a team led by Lindell Bromham studied many more recipes. They found that spice use follows other things as closely as it follows heat. It does not match the risk of illness from food. The amounts of spice in a dish are also much smaller than the amounts used in the laboratory tests.
challenging.context: This card is about whether spicy food is a way of preserving food.

challenging.claim: Eating fermented foods improves the microbes in your gut.
challenging.who: Some scientists, and many makers of probiotic drinks
challenging.for: In one ten-week study, adults who ate more fermented foods ended with more kinds of gut microbes.
challenging.against: The study had only 36 people. Other studies found that swallowed bacteria settle in some people and pass through others. Nobody yet knows how long any change lasts.
challenging.context: This card is about whether curd, kanji and other fermented foods change the microbes living in the gut.

big_questions.q: To a mould, an old lemon is dinner and a home. To us the lemon is spoiled. Who decides what 'spoiled' means?
big_questions.hint: Think about who is using the word, and what they wanted the lemon for.

big_questions.q: Honey feels wet to your finger, but for a yeast cell honey is too dry to live in. So is honey wet or dry?
big_questions.hint: Think about what 'wet' measures: the water that is there, or the water someone can use.

big_questions.q: A mould spore on a dry papad can wait for a year and then grow. Is the spore alive while waiting?
big_questions.hint: List what living things do. Which of those is the waiting spore doing?

big_questions.q: When you set curd, you help one kind of microbe so that others cannot grow. Are you stopping life, or choosing which life?
big_questions.hint: Compare a bowl of curd with a tin of food that was heated until nothing in it was alive.

big_questions.q: About one-third of the food grown in the world is lost or wasted. Microbes eat most of what we throw away. Is that food wasted?
big_questions.hint: Think about who needed the food, what it cost to grow, and what happens to it in the soil.

big_questions.q: Your gut microbes eat the fibre that you are unable to digest, and feed your gut wall. When you eat lunch, who is being fed?
big_questions.hint: Count everyone who gets something from one plate of rice and sambar.

story.title: The Wet Spoon
story.note: Sravani, Karthik and Ammamma are made up. These facts are real. Avakaya is the mango pickle of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. It is made in May from raw mango, salt, mustard powder, chilli powder and oil. Families keep it for a year in a tall ceramic jar called a jaadi. Many homes follow the rules about dry mangoes, dry jars, dry spoons and a layer of oil over the pieces. White mould can grow on pickle pieces that stick out above the oil.
text: Every May, Ammamma made avakaya, the mango pickle that her family in Tenali ate all year. This year Sravani, who was ten, was allowed to help. Her cousin Karthik, who was eight, was allowed to carry things.

Ammamma had rules. There were so many that Sravani counted them on her fingers. Wipe each mango dry with a cloth. Never wash the pieces after cutting. Put the big jar in the sun for a whole day before filling it. Dry your hands. Dry the ladle. And pour oil until it stands two fingers above the mango.
'Why two fingers?' asked Sravani.
'Because my mother did it that way,' said Ammamma, 'and her pickle never spoiled.'
That was not a reason, thought Sravani. But she poured the oil.

They filled the tall brown jar, the jaadi, for the storeroom. Ammamma tied a clean cloth over its mouth. Then she filled one small glass jar for the dining table, so that nobody would open the big jaadi every day.

For three weeks the pickle was wonderful. It was red and sharp, and it turned plain curd rice into a feast. Karthik ate it at every meal. He fetched the small jar himself, and he was careful. Before each meal he washed the pickle spoon at the tap, so that it would be clean.
Then the first rain came. The air turned heavy, and the papads in the tin went soft. One morning Ammamma opened the small jar and stood very still.
'Someone has put a hand in this,' she said.
Sravani looked. On top of the pickle sat a patch of white fuzz, like a scrap of cotton.
'I never used my hand!' said Karthik. His eyes filled with tears. 'I used the spoon. I washed it every time.'
Ammamma reached for the jar, to throw the pickle out.
'Wait,' said Sravani. 'Please. Let me look first.'

She carried the jar to the window. The fuzz was not everywhere. The oil had gone down, because three weeks of spoonfuls had taken oil out with the mango. A few pieces now stuck up above the oil, like rocks above a pond. The white fuzz grew on those pieces and nowhere else. Under the oil, the pickle was as red and clean as on the first day.
Then she looked at the spoon in Karthik's hand. It was shining wet. A drop of water hung from its tip.
Sravani ran to the storeroom and untied the cloth on the big jaadi. The oil stood two fingers above the mango. There was no fuzz at all. Nobody had put a spoon into this jar since May.

She walked back slowly, thinking. The mangoes were the same. The salt and the mustard were the same, and both jars were filled on the same day. One jar was fine and one was not. So what was different? The small jar had been opened every day. Its oil had gone down. And every day a spoon had gone into it, wet from the tap.
'Karthik,' she said, 'you didn't make the pickle dirty. You made it wet.'
'But water is clean!' said Karthik.

'It is clean for us,' said Sravani. 'Think of the papads. They were fine all summer. Then the air turned damp, and they went soft. Ammamma said they would grow fungus if we left them like that. A fungus needs water. The pickle is so salty that it has no water a fungus is able to use. Then your spoon brought fresh water, a few drops every day. And the top pieces were out in the air.'
Ammamma was listening now. Sravani held up her fingers again.
'Wipe the mangoes dry. Dry jar. Dry hands. Dry ladle. Those are all one rule, Ammamma. Keep water out. And the oil two fingers high is the second rule. Keep air out.'
'My mother only said that pickle hates water,' said Ammamma. 'She never said why.'
'She knew what worked,' said Sravani. 'She must have watched which jars kept and which jars spoiled.'

Ammamma threw away all the pickle in the small jar, even the part that looked clean. 'Once the fungus is in, we do not eat from that jar,' she said. She washed the jar with hot water and stood it in the sun. The next day she filled it again from the big jaadi, with a dry ladle, and poured oil until every piece was covered.
Karthik made a label and tied it to the spoon with thread. It said: DRY SPOON ONLY. Then he added a line underneath, in smaller letters.
Washed is not the same as dry.
story.epiphany: Each of the grandmother's pickle rules kept water or air away from microbes. A washed spoon was free of dirt, but it carried fresh water, which was the one thing the mould needed.
ask: The spoon was washed and clean. Why did the pickle still grow mould?
The mould grew only on the pieces above the oil. What does that tell you about what a mould needs?
Which rules in your own kitchen keep water or air away from food?

games.title: Which Hurdle? A card game about how foods are kept
games.context: This is a card game about how foods are kept. Each card names a preserved food. You say which hurdle keeps that food from spoiling: dry, salt, sugar, sour, no air, cold, or heat and seal.

printables.title: 24 food cards to cut out (the hurdles are on the back)

items.f: Papad (appalam)
items.b: DRY. Also SALT. Keep the tin closed, or the papad takes water from the air.

items.f: Avakaya, the mango pickle of Andhra Pradesh
items.b: SALT. Also SOUR mango and NO AIR under the oil.

items.f: Mixed fruit jam, unopened
items.b: SUGAR. Also HEAT AND SEAL. Jam is about two-thirds sugar.

items.f: Honey
items.b: SUGAR. Honey is about one-sixth water, and the sugar holds almost all of it.

items.f: Dried salted fish from the Kerala coast
items.b: DRY. Also SALT.

items.f: Curd in the fridge
items.b: SOUR. Also COLD. Curd bacteria made the acid.

items.f: Long-life milk in an unopened carton
items.b: HEAT AND SEAL. Heated to about 140 degrees and packed with no microbes.

items.f: A packet of pasteurised milk in the fridge
items.b: COLD. The milk was also heated, but a few microbes are left.

items.f: Ghee
items.b: DRY. The water in the butter was boiled away, so almost none is left.

items.f: Raisins
items.b: DRY. Also SUGAR. A raisin is a grape with most of the water gone.

items.f: Amla murabba from Uttar Pradesh
items.b: SUGAR. The amla sits in thick sugar syrup.

items.f: Lemon pickle made with salt only
items.b: SALT. Also SOUR lemon.

items.f: Frozen peas
items.b: COLD. In a freezer there is no liquid water, so microbes stop.

items.f: Raw rice in a dabba
items.b: DRY. Cook the rice, which adds water, and it spoils in a day.

items.f: Rasgulla in a sealed tin
items.b: HEAT AND SEAL. Also SUGAR syrup.

items.f: Tomato sauce in a bottle
items.b: SOUR vinegar. Also SUGAR, SALT, and HEAT AND SEAL.

items.f: Gundruk, the fermented greens of Sikkim
items.b: SOUR, from fermenting. Then DRY, in the sun.

items.f: Vathal from Tamil Nadu
items.b: DRY. Also SALT.

items.f: Milk powder
items.b: DRY. Add water, and it must be used like fresh milk.

items.f: Kokum from the Konkan coast
items.b: DRY. Also SALT and SOUR.

items.f: Chhurpi, the hard cheese of Ladakh and Sikkim
items.b: DRY. So hard and dry that it keeps for years.

items.f: Idli batter in the fridge
items.b: COLD. Also SOUR, from the bacteria in the batter.

items.f: Onions in vinegar
items.b: SOUR. Also SALT.

items.f: Biscuits in an unopened packet
items.b: DRY. The packet is airtight, so no water gets in from the air.

printables.title: A mat with seven spaces
items: SALT: the salt holds the water
SUGAR: the sugar holds the water
NO AIR: under oil or airtight
HEAT AND SEAL: microbes killed, none can enter

rules: Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, food side up.
On your turn, read the top card aloud. Say the main hurdle that keeps this food, and say what the microbes are missing.
Turn the card over. The main hurdle is the first word in capitals. If you named it, keep the card.
If you also named another hurdle on the back, take one extra turn.
If you did not name the main hurdle, put the card on its space on the mat.
When the pile is finished, the player with the most cards wins.
Playing alone: try to keep 18 or more of the 24 cards. Then play again and beat your score.

setup.caption: 1. Put the pile of cards beside the mat.

setup.art: A child holding up a card that says Honey and pointing to the Sugar space on the mat.
setup.caption: 2. Read a card. Say the main hurdle and what the microbes are missing.

setup.caption: 3. Turn the card over to check.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cards and the mat. 2. Read the seven spaces on the mat aloud. 3. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile, food side up.
flow.say: Every preserved food has one or more hurdles that stop microbes from growing in it. There are seven hurdles on the mat. Let us see if we can tell which food uses which.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and the mat. Read the seven hurdles. Mix the cards and make a pile.
flow.context: This is the first step of Which Hurdle? Here you set up the food cards and the mat of seven hurdles.

flow.do: 1. Take turns to read the top card. 2. Say the main hurdle and what the microbes are missing. 3. Turn the card over to check.
flow.say: Read the card aloud. Which hurdle keeps this food? What are the microbes missing: water, warmth, air, or a place that is not too sour?
flow.kid: Read the card. Say the main hurdle. Say what the microbes are missing. Then turn it over.

ask.q: Honey and jam are wet. Why are they on the SUGAR space and not the DRY space?
good: They have water, but the sugar holds it.
Sugar and drying both leave too little free water.

flow.parent: A good answer names what the microbes lack. 'Because it is in a jar' is not enough, so ask what the jar keeps out. Your child may name a true hurdle that is not first on the back. Count that as the extra hurdle.
flow.context: This is the main part of Which Hurdle? Here you read each food card and name the hurdle that keeps microbes from growing in that food.

flow.do: 1. Count your cards. 2. Look at the cards on the mat together. 3. Talk about the ones that surprised you.
flow.say: Which cards went to the mat? What fooled us about them? Which food uses the most hurdles?
flow.kid: Count your cards. Which food surprised you most? Say why.

check.q: Ghee and butter are both made from milk fat. Why does ghee keep without a fridge, when butter does not?
options: Ghee has more salt than butter
The water in butter was boiled away
Ghee is yellow, and microbes avoid yellow food
check.why: Butter is about one-sixth water, so microbes can grow in butter. Making ghee boils that water away and removes the milk solids. With almost no water, almost nothing grows.

flow.context: This is the last step of Which Hurdle? Here you count your cards and talk about the foods that surprised you.

games.title: Food Detective: spoiled, fermented or only changed?
games.context: This is a guessing game with clue cards. Each card describes a change in a food, one clue at a time. You decide whether the food is spoiled, fermented, or only changed without microbes.

printables.title: 12 case cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: Clue 1: A white liquid turned thick overnight. Clue 2: It smells pleasantly sour. Clue 3: Someone stirred in a spoon of yesterday's batch and kept it warm.
items.b: FERMENTED. This is curd. Curd bacteria were added on purpose, and they made acid from the milk sugar.

items.f: Clue 1: A cut fruit went brown in 20 minutes. Clue 2: It has no new smell and no fuzz. Clue 3: Lemon juice would have slowed the browning.
items.b: ONLY CHANGED. This is a cut apple. Substances in the apple reacted with oxygen in the air. No microbe was needed.

items.f: Clue 1: Blue-green fuzzy spots appeared. Clue 2: It sat for a week in a closed bag in damp weather. Clue 3: It smells musty.
items.b: SPOILED. This is mouldy bread. The bag held the dampness in, and mould spores grew.

items.f: Clue 1: It rose to nearly double overnight. Clue 2: It is full of small bubbles and smells a little sour. Clue 3: It was ground from rice and urad dal.
items.b: FERMENTED. This is idli batter. Bacteria and yeasts in the batter made gas and acid.

items.f: Clue 1: It was crisp, and now it bends. Clue 2: It has no spots and no smell. Clue 3: The tin was left open in the monsoon.
items.b: ONLY CHANGED. This is a soft biscuit or papad. It took in water from damp air. Mould may come next.

items.f: Clue 1: A fried snack smells like old paint. Clue 2: It is dry and crisp, with no spots. Clue 3: The packet has been open for two months.
items.b: ONLY CHANGED. The oil has gone rancid. Oxygen from the air changed the oil. Microbes did not.

items.f: Clue 1: It was cooked yesterday afternoon and left on the counter. Clue 2: There is froth on top. Clue 3: It smells sharp and sour.
items.b: SPOILED. This is dal or sambar. Bacteria multiplied in the warm, wet food. Throw it away.

items.f: Clue 1: The skin has turned black in patches. Clue 2: The inside is softer and sweeter. Clue 3: It smells stronger of the fruit.
items.b: ONLY CHANGED. This is a ripe banana. Ripening is the fruit's own work.

items.f: Clue 1: It was runny, and now it is grainy and stiff. Clue 2: The smell and taste are the same. Clue 3: It turns runny again when the jar stands in warm water.
items.b: ONLY CHANGED. This is honey. The sugar has formed crystals. Honey like this is not spoiled.

items.f: Clue 1: A sealed tin has swollen ends. Clue 2: The tin is past its date. Clue 3: Nothing has got in from outside.
items.b: SPOILED. Bacteria that grow without air are making gas inside. Never open or taste it.

items.f: Clue 1: Pale shoots are growing from it. Clue 2: The skin is a little wrinkled. Clue 3: It sat in a dark basket for a month.
items.b: ONLY CHANGED. This is a potato or an onion. They are alive and have started to grow. Cut away any green parts of a potato before cooking.

items.f: Clue 1: Hot milk split into white lumps and pale green water. Clue 2: It happened in one minute. Clue 3: Someone squeezed a lemon into the milk.
items.b: ONLY CHANGED. Acid from the lemon curdled the milk. This is how paneer is made. No microbe was needed.

printables.title: A score sheet
items: Right verdict but wrong reason: 0 points

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes a card and keeps the back hidden.
The reader reads clue 1 aloud. The detective may guess, or ask for the next clue.
A guess has two parts: the verdict (spoiled, fermented, or only changed) and the reason.
The detective gets one guess for each card. A right guess after clue 1 scores 3 points. After clue 2 it scores 2 points, and after clue 3 it scores 1 point.
After six cards, swap places. The player with more points wins.
Playing with a parent: the parent reads all twelve cards. Try to score 24 points or more.

setup.caption: 2. Hear one clue at a time. Guess when you are ready.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 12 cards. 2. Explain the three verdicts: spoiled, fermented, only changed. 3. Decide who reads first.
flow.say: A food detective asks three questions. Did someone set this to ferment? Is there fuzz, slime, froth or a bad smell? Could air or water alone have done it?
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. There are three verdicts: spoiled, fermented, or only changed. Choose who reads first.
flow.context: This is the first step of Food Detective. Here you learn the three verdicts: spoiled, fermented, or only changed without microbes.

flow.do: 1. The reader reads clue 1. 2. The detective guesses or asks for another clue. 3. A guess must give the verdict and the reason. 4. Turn the card and score.
flow.say: Here is the first clue. Do you want to guess now, or hear another clue? Give me your verdict and your reason.
flow.kid: Listen to the clue. Guess now, or ask for one more. Say your verdict and your reason.

ask.q: Risen idli batter and frothy dal both have bubbles and smell sour. How do you tell them apart?
good: The batter was set to ferment on purpose, with microbes we wanted.
Nobody chose the microbes in the dal, and the smell is sharp and bad.

flow.parent: Accept any reason that names what did the changing: wanted microbes, unwanted microbes, air, water from the air, or the food's own growth.
flow.context: This is the main part of Food Detective. Here you hear clues about a changed food and decide whether it is spoiled, fermented or only changed.

flow.do: 1. Add up the points. 2. Ask your child to sort the 12 cards into three piles by verdict. 3. Count each pile.
flow.say: Sort the cards into spoiled, fermented and only changed. How many of the changes needed no microbes at all?
flow.kid: Add up your points. Sort the cards into three piles. How many needed no microbes?
flow.parent: The piles are: 3 spoiled, 2 fermented and 7 only changed.

check.q: A cut apple goes brown in 20 minutes. Is the apple spoiled?
options: Yes, microbes turned the apple brown
No, the apple reacted with oxygen in air
Yes, any change in colour means spoiled
check.why: Browning is a reaction between the apple and oxygen. It happens far too fast for microbes to have grown, and the apple is safe. Colour alone does not tell you that food is spoiled.

flow.context: This is the last step of Food Detective. Here you sort the twelve cases into spoiled, fermented and only changed.

experiments.title: The Salt Ladder: how much salt stops dal water from spoiling?
experiments.context: In this experiment you put the same dal water into five glasses, with more salt in each one. Over three days you find out how much salt it takes to stop the dal water from spoiling.
experiments.question: Does a little salt stop microbes, or is a lot of salt needed? How much salt in 100 millilitres of dal water keeps it from spoiling for three days?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Five glasses of dal water get no salt, a quarter teaspoon, 1 teaspoon, 2 teaspoons and 4 teaspoons. Which glasses will spoil, and which will spoil first? Is there a glass that will not spoil at all? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: Every glass gets dal water from the same pot, in the same amount, in the same kind of glass. All five stand open in the same air for the same 30 minutes. Then they sit side by side in the same place. Only the amount of salt changes. Stir from the least salty glass to the most salty, so the spoon carries no extra salt backwards.
results_table: Number of the check when it first spoiled

materials.item: toor dal or moong dal
water
fine table salt
clear glasses or clean glass jars, all the same size
saucers or small plates to cover the glasses
a measuring cup, a marked baby bottle, or a medicine cup marked in millilitres
a teaspoon, a strainer and a small pan
paper, tape and a pen for labels, and a page of newspaper

experiments.safety: A grown-up boils and strains the dal. Never taste anything from the glasses, not even on the first day. Smell by waving your hand over the glass towards your nose, not by putting your nose in. At the end, pour everything down the sink and wash the glasses with soap and hot water.

schedule.what: Boil and strain the dal water. Guess. Fill five glasses, add the salt, leave them open for 30 minutes, then cover them. Do the first check in the evening.
Check all five glasses in the morning and in the evening. Look, smell by waving, and write what you find.
Check all five glasses in the morning and in the evening.
Do the last check. Draw the bar chart, say what you found, and wash everything.

experiments.record: Fill in the table at every check. Write 'same' if a glass looks and smells as it did at the start. Write what changed if it is cloudier, frothy, has a skin on top or smells sour or bad. Then draw a bar chart of the check at which each glass first spoiled. Write one sentence saying what you found (your claim). Write one giving the checks that show it (your evidence). Write one saying why you think it happened (your reasoning).

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: the check at which each glass first spoiled
example_chart.x: Salt in 100 ml of dal water
example_chart.y: Number of the check (7 means it never spoiled)
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished chart can look like. A taller bar means the dal water kept for longer. Your results will be different.

setup.caption: 1. A grown-up boils dal in water and strains it. Let the dal water cool.

setup.art: Five clear glasses in a row labelled A to E, each with the same amount of pale dal water, and a teaspoon of salt held above glass C.
setup.caption: 2. Pour 100 ml into each glass. Add no salt, a quarter, 1, 2 and 4 teaspoons.

setup.caption: 3. Leave them open for 30 minutes. Then cover them and keep them together.

setup.caption: 4. Twice a day, look for cloudiness, froth and a new smell. Write it down.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up boils 2 tablespoons of dal in 700 ml of water for 15 minutes. 2. Strain the water into a jug and keep the dal for cooking. 3. Let the dal water cool until it is just warm. 4. While it cools, write labels A, B, C, D and E.
flow.say: We need a food that microbes like. Dal water has food and water in it. Let's make some and let it cool.
flow.kid: A grown-up boils the dal and strains it. Let the dal water cool. Write five labels: A, B, C, D and E.
flow.parent: The dal water should be thin and you should be able to see through it a little. If it is thick, add boiled water. Cooling takes about 30 minutes, so start the guessing step while you wait.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Salt Ladder. Here a grown-up makes dal water, the food that the microbes will grow in.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the five labels and the salt. 2. Tell them how much salt each glass will get. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason, and write both down.
flow.say: Glass A gets no salt. B gets a quarter teaspoon, C gets 1, D gets 2 and E gets 4. Which will spoil? Which will spoil first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Glass A gets no salt. Glass E gets the most. Which glasses will spoil? Which one first? Say why. Write your guess.

ask.q: We put a little salt in dal when we cook it. Do you think that salt helps the dal keep?
good: Maybe a little.
No, because cooked dal with salt still spoils by the next day.

flow.parent: Many children guess that any salt will help, and that more salt helps a little more each time. Do not correct the guess. The glasses will answer.
flow.context: This step of the Salt Ladder is for guessing. You guess which of five glasses of dal water, each with a different amount of salt, will spoil.

flow.do: 1. Pour 100 ml of cool dal water into each glass. 2. Add salt: none to A, a quarter teaspoon to B, 1 level teaspoon to C, 2 to D and 4 to E. 3. Stir A first, then B, C, D and E, until the salt has dissolved. 4. Stick on the labels.
flow.say: Measure carefully. Every glass must get the same dal water, so that only the salt is different. Level each teaspoon with your finger.
flow.kid: Pour 100 ml into each glass. Add the salt for each label. Stir glass A first and glass E last. Stick the labels on.
flow.parent: One level teaspoon of fine salt weighs about 6 grams. So the five glasses hold about 0, 1.5, 6, 12 and 24 grams of salt in 100 ml. The salt in glass E takes a minute or two of stirring to dissolve.
flow.context: In this step of the Salt Ladder you fill five glasses with the same dal water. You add a different amount of salt to each.

flow.do: 1. Stand all five glasses side by side, open, for 30 minutes. 2. Then cover each with a saucer. 3. Put them together on a shelf, away from the sun and the stove. 4. In the evening, do check 1: hold newspaper behind each glass, look, and smell by waving.
flow.say: Microbes from the air and the spoon are in every glass now. We leave them all open for the same time, so each gets the same chance.
flow.kid: Leave the glasses open for 30 minutes. Then cover each one with a saucer. In the evening, look and smell. Write what you find.

ask.q: Why do we leave all five open for the same time?
good: So the same air and the same microbes reach each glass.
So that only the salt is different.

flow.parent: The salty glasses may look a little different from the start. That is why check 1 matters: later you compare each glass with how that same glass looked on day 1.
flow.context: In this step of the Salt Ladder you let the same air reach all five glasses and cover them. You also write down how they look at the start.

flow.do: 1. Every morning and evening for the next two days, lift each saucer. 2. Look through the glass at the newspaper: is the print harder to read than before? 3. Look for bubbles, froth or a skin on top. 4. Wave the air towards your nose: is there a sour or bad smell? 5. Write it in the table. Never taste.
flow.say: Look, then smell by waving. What has changed in each glass since the last check? Which glass changed first?
flow.kid: Twice a day, check each glass. Is it cloudier? Is there froth? Does it smell sour? Write it down. Never taste.

ask.q: Glass B has some salt. Is it keeping better than glass A?
good: No, they look about the same.
Only a little, or not at all.

flow.parent: In a warm kitchen, glasses A and B usually turn cloudy and smell sour by check 2 or 3. Glass C often spoils later, or not within three days. D and E usually stay as they were. In a cool room everything is slower, so go on for two more days.
flow.wait: Check every morning and evening on day 2 and day 3
flow.context: This step of the Salt Ladder is repeated twice a day for two days. You look at and smell five glasses of dal water with different amounts of salt.

flow.do: 1. On the morning of day 4, do the last check. 2. For each glass, find the number of the check at which it first spoiled. If it never spoiled, write 7. 3. Draw a bar chart with one bar for each glass. 4. Ask your child the question below. 5. Pour everything away and wash up with soap and hot water.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Then tell me: how much salt was enough?
flow.kid: Do the last check. Draw a bar for each glass. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: Glass E is still mostly water. Why did microbes not grow there?
good: The salt holds on to the water, so the microbes are unable to take any in.
Water moves out of the microbes into the salty water.

ask.q: Pickle is very salty. Could we make pickle with only a little salt?
good: No. A little salt did not stop the dal water from spoiling.
It would spoil unless something else, like the fridge or sourness, helped.

flow.parent: If glass C spoiled late, point to it: it shows that the change from 'spoils' to 'keeps' happens somewhere between 1 and 2 teaspoons. That is 6 to 12 grams in 100 ml, about the strength of pickling brine.

check.q: In the Salt Ladder, a quarter teaspoon of salt did not slow the spoiling. What does that show?
options: Salt has no effect on microbes
A little salt is too little to stop microbes
That glass was dirtier than the others
check.why: A little salt leaves plenty of free water, so microbes grow as usual. Only a large amount of salt holds enough water to stop them. Salt does affect microbes, as the saltiest glasses showed. And the test was fair: every glass had the same dal water and the same air.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Salt Ladder. Here you draw a bar chart of when each glass of dal water spoiled, and explain what the chart shows.

experiments.title: Thick or Thin: can jaggery water be too sweet to spoil?
experiments.context: In this experiment you make jaggery water at three strengths: thin, medium and a thick syrup. Over five days you find out which ones ferment. Then you thin the thick syrup with water to see what changes.
experiments.question: Yeasts eat sugar. So does more sugar mean more fermenting, or can there be so much sugar that the yeasts stop?
experiments.predict: Guess first. One glass has a little jaggery in a lot of water. One has more jaggery. One is a thick syrup with very little water. Which will bubble and smell fermented first? Which will change the least? Why do you think so? Write your guess and your reason.
experiments.fair_test: All three glasses get jaggery from one block, the same small pinch of atta and the same kind of cover. They stand side by side. Only the share of jaggery to water changes.
results_table: First day with bubbles or a new smell

materials.item: jaggery, grated or powdered (sugar also works)
drinking water at room warmth
hot water, poured by a grown-up
atta (whole wheat flour)
clear glasses or small clean jars
pieces of thin cotton cloth and rubber bands, or saucers, to cover the glasses
a tablespoon, a teaspoon, labels and a pen

experiments.safety: A grown-up pours the hot water. Do not taste or drink anything from the glasses. Fermented jaggery water holds a little alcohol and may grow mould. Keep the glasses covered, so flies and ants stay out. At the end, pour everything down the sink.

schedule.what: Guess. Mix the thin, medium and thick glasses. Add a pinch of atta to each, cover them and put them in a warm place.
Look for bubbles, froth and cloudiness, and smell by waving. Write what you find.
Check and write again.
Check and write again.
Do the last check and say what you found. Then thin one spoon of the thick syrup with water in a new glass.
Look at the thinned glass after three days. Write what you find, and pour everything away.

experiments.record: Each day, write for each glass: bubbles (yes or no), froth or skin on top (yes or no), smell (same, sour, fruity or bad). Circle the first day each glass changed. At the end, write what you found (your claim), which days show it (your evidence) and why you think it happened (your reasoning).

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
example_chart.note: These results are made up, to show how to fill in the table. Yours will be different.

setup.art: Three clear glasses labelled Thin, Medium and Thick, holding pale brown, darker brown and very dark thick jaggery liquid, with a block of jaggery and a tablespoon beside them.
setup.caption: 1. Mix jaggery and water at three strengths.

setup.art: A child's fingers dropping a small pinch of atta into the glass labelled Thin, with a small bowl of atta nearby.
setup.caption: 2. Stir a small pinch of atta into each glass. Atta carries wild yeasts.

setup.art: The three glasses covered with thin cloth held by rubber bands, on a shelf in a warm kitchen.
setup.caption: 3. Cover each glass with cloth. Keep them together in a warm place.

setup.art: The Thin glass with froth and bubbles on top, beside the Thick glass looking unchanged, and a child writing in a table.
setup.caption: 4. Check once a day for five days. Never taste.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the jaggery, the water and the three labels: Thin, Medium, Thick. 2. Say how each will be mixed. 3. Ask for a guess and a reason. Write both down.
flow.say: Yeasts eat sugar and make bubbles. One glass will have a little jaggery, one more, and one will be thick syrup. Which will ferment first? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Yeasts eat sugar. One glass is thin, one is medium, one is thick syrup. Which will bubble first? Say why. Write your guess.
flow.parent: Most children guess the thick syrup, because it has the most food for the yeasts. That is a sensible guess. Do not correct it.
flow.context: This step of Thick or Thin is for guessing. You guess which of three strengths of jaggery water will ferment first.

flow.do: 1. Thin: stir 1 tablespoon of jaggery into 8 tablespoons of water. 2. Medium: stir 4 tablespoons of jaggery into 8 tablespoons of water. 3. Thick: put 8 tablespoons of jaggery in the third glass. A grown-up adds 3 tablespoons of hot water. Stir until it is a thick syrup, and let it cool. 4. Label the glasses.
flow.say: Count the spoons aloud as you measure. The thin glass has 1 spoon of jaggery to 8 of water. The thick one has 8 of jaggery to 3 of water.
flow.kid: Mix the thin glass and the medium glass. A grown-up adds hot water to the thick glass. Stir each one well. Stick the labels on.
flow.parent: The thick syrup should pour slowly, like honey. A few grains of jaggery left at the bottom do not matter. Let it cool before the next step, because heat would kill the yeasts.
flow.context: In this step of Thick or Thin you mix jaggery and water at three strengths: thin, medium and a thick syrup.

flow.do: 1. Add one small pinch of atta to each glass, the same size each time. 2. Stir each with a clean spoon. 3. Cover each glass with thin cloth and a rubber band. 4. Put all three in a warm place out of the sun.
flow.say: Atta carries wild yeasts and bacteria, as fresh grain does. Now every glass has the same microbes. Only the share of jaggery and water is different.
flow.kid: Add a small pinch of atta to each glass. Stir. Cover each glass with cloth. Put them in a warm place.

ask.q: Why must every glass get the same pinch of atta?
good: So every glass starts with the same microbes.
Otherwise we would not know whether the atta or the jaggery made the difference.

flow.context: In this step of Thick or Thin you add the same pinch of atta to three glasses of jaggery water. Atta carries wild yeasts.

flow.do: 1. Once a day for the next three days, look at each glass through its side. 2. Look for bubbles rising, froth on top and cloudiness. 3. Lift the cloth and smell by waving. 4. Write it in the table. Do not stir and do not taste.
flow.say: What has changed since yesterday? Look for bubbles first. Then smell by waving your hand. Is the smell sour, fruity or the same?
flow.kid: Once a day, check each glass. Are there bubbles? Is there froth? Is the smell new? Write it down. Never taste.
flow.parent: In a warm kitchen the thin glass usually bubbles and smells sour or fruity within two or three days. The medium glass often follows a day later. The thick syrup usually stays the same. In a cool room, allow up to a week. A white skin or spots of mould on the thin glass also count as a change.
flow.wait: Check once a day on days 2, 3 and 4
flow.context: This step of Thick or Thin is repeated once a day for three days. You look for bubbles and new smells in three strengths of jaggery water.

flow.do: 1. On day 5, do the last check. 2. Circle the first day each glass changed. 3. Ask your child to explain the result, and ask the questions below.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The thick glass had the most sugar. So why did the yeasts not grow there?
flow.kid: Do the last check. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: The thick syrup had the most food for yeasts. Why did it change the least?
good: There was too little water that the yeasts could use.
The sugar holds on to the water.
Water moves out of the yeast cells into the syrup.

ask.q: How could we test whether the thick syrup harms the yeasts, or is only short of water?
good: Add water to some of the thick syrup and see if it ferments then.

flow.parent: If your child suggests adding water to the thick syrup, they have designed the next step themselves. Say so.

check.q: In Thick or Thin, thin jaggery water fermented but thick jaggery syrup did not. Why?
options: Thick syrup has no food for yeasts
In thick syrup, sugar holds the water
Yeasts dislike the colour of thick syrup
check.why: Thick syrup is full of food, but the sugar holds on to nearly all the water. A yeast cell in thick syrup loses water and stops growing. Thin jaggery water has the same food and plenty of free water.

flow.context: In this step of Thick or Thin you compare three strengths of jaggery water after five days. You explain which ones fermented.

flow.do: 1. Put 1 tablespoon of the thick syrup into a clean fourth glass. 2. Stir in 8 tablespoons of water, and add nothing else. 3. Label it 'Thick, thinned' and cover it. 4. Keep it beside the old thick glass. 5. Check both once a day for three more days. Then pour everything away.
flow.say: Now we test your idea. This is the same syrup that did not ferment. We add only water. What do you think will happen? Why?
flow.kid: Take one spoon of the thick syrup. Add 8 spoons of water and nothing else. Watch it for three days.

ask.q: The thinned syrup fermented. What does that tell you about the thick syrup?
good: Nothing in the jaggery was stopping the yeasts.
The thick syrup was only short of free water.

flow.parent: The thinned glass usually ferments within two or three days, like the first thin glass. This is the strongest evidence in the experiment, because the only thing added was water.
flow.wait: Check the thinned glass once a day for three more days
flow.context: This is the last step of Thick or Thin. The thick jaggery syrup did not ferment. So here you add water to one spoon of that syrup and see whether it ferments now.

experiments.title: Sun-Dried Tomato: how much of a tomato is water?
experiments.context: In this experiment you dry some tomato slices in the sun and seal other slices in a jar. You weigh the drying slices every day, and you find out which slices spoil.
experiments.question: How much of a tomato's weight is water? And which will spoil first: slices sealed in a clean jar, or slices left in the open sun?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Six tomato slices will dry in the sun for three days. Will they end at about half their weight, a quarter, or less? Three more slices will be sealed in a clean jar. Which will spoil first, the open slices or the sealed ones? Why do you think so? Write your guesses and your reasons.
experiments.fair_test: All the slices come from the same tomatoes and are cut to the same thickness. Only one thing differs. One set loses water in the sun and moving air. The other set keeps all its water in a closed jar.
results_table: Weight of the six sun slices (grams)
How the sun slices look and feel

materials.item: firm, ripe tomatoes
a knife and a cutting board, used by a grown-up
a steel plate
a thin cotton cloth or a net food cover, and four clothes pegs or small stones
a small clear jar with a lid, or a zip bag
a kitchen scale. If you have none, make a hanger balance: a clothes hanger, two identical paper cups, thread, and a 5 ml medicine spoon
a sunny window sill or balcony

experiments.safety: A grown-up does the cutting. These slices are for testing, not for eating. Do not open the jar of sealed slices indoors once they have gone mouldy. Throw a zip bag away closed. Empty a jar straight into the wet waste, at arm's length, and wash it with hot water and soap.

schedule.what: Guess. A grown-up slices the tomatoes. Weigh six slices and put them in the sun under a cloth. Seal three slices in a jar on the kitchen shelf.
Weigh the sun slices and turn them over. Look at the jar slices without opening the jar.
Weigh, turn and look again.
Weigh the sun slices once more. Work out how much water left. Compare the two sets and explain.

experiments.record: Each day, write the weight of the six sun slices, and how both sets look. On day 4, subtract the last weight from the first to find the water that left. Draw a line graph of weight against day. Write what you found (your claim), the numbers that show it (your evidence) and why you think it happened (your reasoning).

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: weight of six tomato slices drying in the sun
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished graph can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A grown-up's hands slicing a red tomato into thin round slices on a cutting board, with nine slices laid out.
setup.caption: 1. A grown-up cuts thin slices, each about as thick as two 5-rupee coins.

setup.art: A clothes hanger hung from a door handle with a paper cup on each end, tomato slices in one cup and a child adding water with a medicine spoon to the other.
setup.caption: 2. Weigh six slices on a scale, or on a hanger balance against spoons of water.

setup.art: A steel plate of tomato slices on a sunny window sill, covered by a thin cloth held up on pegs so it does not touch the slices.
setup.caption: 3. Put six slices in the sun under a thin cloth.

setup.art: A small closed glass jar with three wet tomato slices inside, on a kitchen shelf.
setup.caption: 4. Seal three slices in a clean jar on the shelf. Weigh and look every day.

flow.do: 1. Show your child the tomatoes, the plate and the jar. 2. Ask for both guesses and the reasons. 3. Write them down.
flow.say: Six slices will dry in the sun. How much lighter will they be after three days? And which slices will spoil first, the open ones or the sealed ones? Why?
flow.kid: How much lighter will dried slices be? Which will spoil first: open slices or sealed slices? Say why. Write your guesses.
flow.parent: Many children expect the open slices to spoil first, because flies and dust can reach them. They expect the sealed ones to stay clean. Do not correct the guess.
flow.context: This step of Sun-Dried Tomato is for guessing. You guess how much weight tomato slices lose in the sun, and whether open or sealed slices spoil first.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts both tomatoes into slices about 4 millimetres thick. 2. Choose six slices of about the same size for the sun. 3. Choose three more for the jar. 4. Put the three slices in the clean jar and close the lid.
flow.say: The slices must be thin and even. Thin slices dry fast. Thick ones stay wet in the middle.
flow.kid: A grown-up cuts thin, even slices. Put six on the plate. Put three in the jar. Close the jar.
flow.context: In this step of Sun-Dried Tomato a grown-up cuts thin tomato slices. Six go on a plate to dry and three go in a closed jar.

flow.do: 1. Weigh the six sun slices on a kitchen scale, and write the grams. 2. With no scale, hang a paper cup from each end of a hanger. Hang the hanger from a door handle. 3. Put the slices in one cup. 4. Add water to the other cup with the 5 ml spoon until the hanger is level. 5. Count the spoons. Each spoon is 5 grams.
