flow.say: We need the weight at the start, so we can tell how much water leaves. One 5 ml spoon of water weighs 5 grams.
flow.kid: Weigh the six slices. With no scale, use the hanger balance. Count spoons of water until it is level. Each spoon is 5 grams.
flow.parent: A hanger balance is good to about one spoon, 5 grams. Six slices usually weigh 60 to 90 grams, which is 12 to 18 spoons. Check first that the empty cups hang level. If they do not, add a paper clip to the lighter side.
flow.context: In this step of Sun-Dried Tomato you weigh six tomato slices before they dry. You use a scale or a hanger balance.

flow.do: 1. Spread the six slices on the steel plate, not touching each other. 2. Put the plate in the sunniest place you have. 3. Cover it with thin cloth held up on pegs or stones, so the cloth does not touch the slices. 4. Put the closed jar on a kitchen shelf, not in the fridge.
flow.say: The cloth keeps flies off and lets the air through. The jar stays closed from now on. We only look through the glass.
flow.kid: Spread the slices on the plate. Put it in the sun. Cover it with thin cloth. Put the jar on a shelf.
flow.parent: Bring the plate indoors at night. In the monsoon, or with no sunny spot, put the plate under a ceiling fan. If the open slices still do not dry and begin to grow mould, write that down. It shows why families dry food in the hot, dry months.
flow.context: In this step of Sun-Dried Tomato you put six tomato slices in the sun under a cloth. A jar of three slices goes on a shelf.

flow.do: 1. Each day for two days, weigh the six sun slices and write the weight. 2. Turn each slice over. 3. Feel one slice: is it wet, leathery or crisp? 4. Look at the jar slices through the glass. Look for liquid, slime and fuzz. Do not open the jar.
flow.say: What has changed in the sun slices? What has changed in the jar? Which set still has all its water?
flow.kid: Weigh the sun slices each day. Turn them over. Look at the jar slices. Do not open the jar. Write it all down.
flow.parent: The sun slices usually lose more than half their weight on the first sunny day. The jar slices usually sit in a pool of juice by day 2 or 3. They may show slime or fuzz by day 3 to 5.
flow.wait: Weigh and look once a day on day 2 and day 3
flow.context: This step of Sun-Dried Tomato is repeated on two days. You weigh the tomato slices drying in the sun, and look at the slices sealed in the jar.

flow.do: 1. On day 4, weigh the sun slices once more. 2. Subtract the last weight from the first weight. That is the water that left. 3. Draw a line graph of the four weights. 4. Compare the sun slices with the jar slices. 5. Put the dried slices in a dry, closed jar, and look at them again in a week.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. The jar was clean and closed. So why did those slices spoil?
flow.kid: Weigh the dried slices. Subtract to find the water lost. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: The jar was clean and closed. Where did the microbes inside come from?
good: They were already on the tomato skin and the knife.
Microbes are on every food.

ask.q: The dried slices sat in open air with microbes landing on them. Why did they not spoil?
good: They had too little water left for microbes to grow.

ask.q: What would happen if the dried slices got damp again?
good: The microbes waiting on them could start to grow.

flow.parent: A tomato is about 94 parts water in 100. After three days of home drying, slices usually weigh between one-tenth and one-fifth of their starting weight. If your child's result is far from this, ask what could have gone wrong with the weighing.

check.q: In Sun-Dried Tomato, the sealed slices spoiled and the dried slices did not. What explains this best?
options: Sunlight adds a preservative to food
Only the sealed slices kept their water
Air cleans the microbes off food
check.why: Microbes were on both sets from the start. The sealed slices kept all their water, so the microbes grew. The dried slices had too little free water left. Sunlight does kill some microbes on the surface, but dryness is what keeps dried food for months.

flow.context: This is the last step of Sun-Dried Tomato. Here you work out how much water left the dried tomato slices, and explain why the sealed slices spoiled.

activities.title: The Longest-Lasting Shelf: which foods keep, and what are they like?
activities.context: In this activity you search your kitchen for the foods that keep longest and the foods that spoil fastest. Then you look for what the long-lasting foods have in common.

materials.item: your own kitchen shelves and fridge
a notebook page and a pencil
food packets with a 'best before' line on the label

schedule.what: Find eight foods that keep for months and five that spoil within two days. Describe each one, and look for a pattern.

activities.record: Draw a table with three columns: the food, how long it keeps, and what it is like (dry, salty, very sweet, sour, under oil, sealed, or cold). Under the table, write one sentence about what the long-lasting foods have in common.

setup.art: A child standing on a low stool reading the label on a jar taken from a kitchen shelf full of dabbas, jars and packets.
setup.caption: 1. Find eight foods that keep for months. Read the labels.

setup.art: A notebook page with a three-column table half filled in: papad, 9 months, dry and salty.
setup.caption: 2. Write how long each keeps and what it is like.

setup.art: A child pointing at the notebook table, with a pickle jar, a honey jar and a packet of rice on the table.
setup.caption: 3. Look down the last column. What do you notice?

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to find eight foods in the kitchen that keep for months without a fridge. 2. For packets, read the 'best before' line. 3. Write each food and how long it keeps.
flow.say: Which foods in our kitchen have been here the longest? Find eight that keep for months. Read the label where there is one.
flow.kid: Find eight foods that keep for months. Read the 'best before' line on packets. Write each food and how long it keeps.
flow.parent: Good finds are rice, dal, atta, sugar, salt, papad, pickle, jam, honey and ghee. Oil, biscuits, tamarind, jaggery, milk powder and long-life milk in a carton also count.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Longest-Lasting Shelf. Here you find the foods in your kitchen that keep for months.

flow.do: 1. For each long-lasting food, ask what it is like. 2. Let your child feel a grain of rice, and taste a little pickle, jam and tamarind. 3. Write one or more words for each: dry, salty, very sweet, sour, under oil, sealed, cold.
flow.say: Feel it or taste a little. Is it dry? Very salty? Very sweet? Sour? Covered in oil? Sealed in a packet that was never opened?
flow.kid: Feel or taste each food. Is it dry, salty, very sweet, sour or oily? Is it sealed? Write the words.

ask.q: Is there any long-lasting food that is wet, not salty, not sweet, not sour and not sealed?
good: No, I could not find one.

flow.context: In this step of the Longest-Lasting Shelf you describe each long-lasting food: dry, salty, very sweet, sour, oily or sealed.

flow.do: 1. Now ask for five foods that spoil within two days outside the fridge. 2. Describe each in the same way. 3. Ask your child what is different about the two lists. Do not explain yet.
flow.say: Now find five foods that spoil within two days on the counter. What are they like? What is different about your two lists? Why do you think that matters?
flow.kid: Find five foods that spoil in two days. What are they like? How do your two lists differ? Say why you think so.

ask.q: What do the fast-spoiling foods have in common?
good: They are wet or soft.
They are cooked.
They are not very salty, sweet or sour.

flow.parent: Your child may notice that every long-lasting food is dry, salty, very sweet, sour, oily, sealed or cold. Write down their own words. The experiments that follow test why.

check.q: Raw rice keeps for a year. Cooked rice spoils in a day. What did cooking change?
options: Cooking added water to the rice
Cooking took the salt out of the rice
Cooking made the rice older
check.why: Dry rice has too little water for microbes to grow. Cooking adds water, and then they can. Rice has almost no salt before or after cooking, and its age has not changed.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Longest-Lasting Shelf. Here you compare foods that spoil fast with foods that keep, and look for the difference.

activities.title: Count the Hurdles: read a pickle jar, a jam jar and a sauce bottle
activities.context: In this activity you read the labels of preserved foods from your kitchen. For each food you count the hurdles. A hurdle is any one thing that keeps that food from spoiling.

materials.item: preserved foods with labels, such as pickle, jam, tomato sauce, squash, papad, biscuits or long-life milk
a notebook page and a pencil

schedule.what: Read the ingredients and storage lines on four or five labels. Tick the hurdles each food uses, and count them.

activities.record: Draw a table. Down the side, write each food. Across the top, write the hurdles: dry, salt, sugar, sour, oil, heated and sealed, added preservative, cold after opening. Tick each hurdle a food uses, and write the total.

setup.art: A pickle jar, a jam jar and a bottle of tomato sauce on a table, turned so their ingredient labels face forward.
setup.caption: 1. Collect four or five preserved foods with labels.

setup.art: A child's finger under the ingredients list on a jam jar, with the first word, sugar, circled.
setup.caption: 2. Read the ingredients. The first one is the biggest by weight.

setup.art: A notebook table with foods down the side, hurdles across the top and ticks in the boxes.
setup.caption: 3. Tick each hurdle. Count the ticks for each food.

flow.do: 1. Collect four or five preserved foods with labels. 2. Find the ingredients list on each. 3. Tell your child that ingredients are listed from the largest amount to the smallest.
flow.say: On a label, the first ingredient is the one there is most of. What comes first on the jam? What comes first on the pickle?
flow.kid: Collect four or five preserved foods. Find the ingredients list on each. The first ingredient is the biggest.
flow.context: This is the first step of Count the Hurdles. Here you collect preserved foods and find the ingredients list on each label.

flow.do: 1. For each food, read the ingredients aloud. 2. Tick the hurdles in the table: dry, salt, sugar, sour, oil, heated and sealed, added preservative, cold after opening. 3. Look for the storage line too, such as 'refrigerate after opening'.
flow.say: Vinegar, acetic acid, citric acid and lemon all make food sour. 'Preservative' with a number is an added one. Which hurdles does this food use?
flow.kid: Read each label aloud. Tick every hurdle the food uses. Look for 'refrigerate after opening' too.
flow.parent: Some help with label words: 'acidity regulator (260)' is the acid of vinegar and '(330)' is the acid of lemons. 'Preservative (211)' is sodium benzoate and '(202)' is potassium sorbate. A jar or bottle that was sealed in a factory was almost always heated first.
flow.context: In this step of Count the Hurdles you read each label. You tick every hurdle that keeps that food from spoiling.

flow.do: 1. Count the ticks for each food. 2. Ask which food uses the most hurdles and which uses only one. 3. Ask the question about the storage line.
flow.say: Which food has the most hurdles? Which keeps with only one? Why does a jar say 'refrigerate after opening' and not before?
flow.kid: Count the ticks. Which food has the most hurdles? Why keep a jar cold only after opening?

ask.q: Honey and dry rice each have only one hurdle. Why is one enough for them?
good: They have so little free water that nothing grows.
That one hurdle is very strong.

flow.parent: A typical tomato sauce uses five hurdles: vinegar, sugar, salt, heating and sealing, and sometimes an added preservative.

check.q: A jam jar says 'refrigerate after opening'. Why is the fridge not needed before opening?
options: Unopened jam has no sugar
The jar was heated and sealed
Jam only spoils in the light
check.why: The jam was heated and sealed. So the jar starts with almost no living microbes, and none can enter. Opening the jar lets spores in from the air and from spoons. The seal was one hurdle, and cold replaces it.

flow.context: This is the last step of Count the Hurdles. Here you compare how many hurdles each preserved food uses.

activities.title: The Snap Test: does dry food stay dry?
activities.context: In this activity you keep three crisp biscuits overnight in three places: an airtight dabba, an open plate and under a bowl with a damp cloth. In the morning you snap each one to find which took in water from the air.

materials.item: crisp, plain biscuits from one packet (or three pieces of one roasted papad)
a small airtight dabba
two plates and a large bowl
a small damp cloth

schedule.what: Guess. Put one biscuit in an airtight dabba and one on an open plate. Put the third under a bowl beside a damp cloth.
Snap each biscuit, listen and feel. Explain where the water came from.

activities.safety: Do not eat the biscuit that sat beside the damp cloth.
activities.record: Write your guess. In the morning, write for each biscuit: did it snap with a sound, or bend? Then write one sentence saying where the water came from.

setup.art: Three identical round biscuits: one inside a small steel dabba with its lid beside it, one on an open plate, one on a plate next to a folded damp cloth.
setup.caption: 1. Put three biscuits in three places.

setup.art: A large bowl turned upside down over the plate with the biscuit and the damp cloth, the cloth not touching the biscuit.
setup.caption: 2. Cover the third biscuit and the damp cloth with a bowl. The cloth must not touch the biscuit.

setup.art: A child's hands snapping one biscuit cleanly in two, with a second biscuit bending without breaking.
setup.caption: 3. Next morning, snap each biscuit. Listen and feel.

flow.do: 1. Snap a spare biscuit first, so your child hears a crisp one. 2. Put biscuit 1 in the airtight dabba and close it. 3. Put biscuit 2 on an open plate. 4. Put biscuit 3 on a plate beside a damp cloth, not touching it. Cover both with an upturned bowl. 5. Ask for a guess and a reason.
flow.say: Nothing wet will touch any of these biscuits. Tomorrow, which will still snap? Which will bend? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Put the three biscuits in their places. Nothing wet touches them. Which will still snap tomorrow? Say why.
flow.parent: The damp cloth must not touch biscuit 3. The point is that water reaches the biscuit only through the air.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Snap Test. Here you put three crisp biscuits in three places overnight and guess which will stay crisp.

flow.do: 1. Next morning, snap each biscuit in turn. 2. Listen for the snap and feel whether it bends. 3. Ask where the water in the soft biscuit came from. 4. Throw away biscuit 3.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. No water touched this biscuit. So how did it get soft?
flow.kid: Snap each biscuit. Which ones bend? Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: How did water reach the biscuit under the bowl?
good: It went into the air from the damp cloth, and from the air into the biscuit.
As water vapour that we do not see.

ask.q: Why do some food packets hold a small sachet that says 'do not eat'?
good: The sachet takes water out of the air in the packet, so the food stays dry.

flow.parent: Biscuit 1 should snap cleanly and biscuit 3 should bend. Biscuit 2 depends on your weather: it softens on a humid night and may stay crisp in dry winter air. Either result is worth talking about.

check.q: A papad in an open tin goes soft, and later grows mould. Why does mould come only after softening?
options: Mould spores arrive only in the rain
Water from the air lets waiting spores grow
Soft papad has more salt
check.why: Mould spores were on the papad all along, waiting. A dry papad has too little free water for them. Damp air gives the papad water, and then the spores grow. The salt in the papad has not changed.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Snap Test. Here you snap three biscuits that spent the night in a dabba, on a plate and beside a damp cloth.

activities.title: The Preserving Map of India
activities.context: In this activity you draw a map of India and place twelve preserved foods on it. They range from dried vegetables in Kashmir to dried fish in Kerala. For each food you name the hurdle that keeps it.

materials.item: a large sheet of paper and pencils or crayons
an atlas or a map of India to copy from
the list of twelve foods in the first step
an older person to ask, at home or by phone

schedule.what: Draw an outline map of India. Place twelve preserved foods on it and name the hurdle for each. Add two foods from your own family.

activities.record: Your map is the record. Beside each food, write the hurdle or hurdles that keep it: dry, salt, sugar, sour, oil, smoke or fermenting.

setup.art: A child copying the outline of India from an atlas on to a large sheet of paper.
setup.caption: 1. Draw a big outline map of India.

setup.art: The map with small drawings placed on it: a string of dried vegetables at the top, a pickle jar in the south-east, drying fish on the south-west coast.
setup.caption: 2. Draw each food where it is made. Write its hurdle.

setup.art: A child on the phone with a grandmother, writing in a notebook beside the map.
setup.caption: 3. Ask an older person for two preserved foods from your family. Add them.

flow.do: 1. Draw a large outline of India. 2. Read the twelve foods to your child, one at a time: hokh syun, dried vegetables of Kashmir. Chhurpi, hard dried cheese of Ladakh. Amla murabba of Uttar Pradesh. Ker sangri, dried desert beans and berries of Rajasthan. Chhundo, mango cooked in sugar, of Gujarat. Kokum, dried salted fruit rind of Konkan and Goa. Avakaya of Andhra Pradesh and Telangana. Vathal of Tamil Nadu. Dried salted fish of Kerala. Badi, sun-dried dal drops of Odisha. Gundruk, fermented and dried greens of Sikkim. Smoked meat of Nagaland. 3. Your child draws each food in the right place.
flow.say: Find each place on the atlas first. Then draw the food there. Before I tell you, guess how each one is kept.
flow.kid: Draw India. Find each place in the atlas. Draw the food there. Guess how each food is kept.
flow.parent: The hurdles are: hokh syun, chhurpi, ker sangri and badi are dried. Murabba and chhundo use sugar. Kokum and dried fish are salted and dried. Avakaya uses salt, sour mango and oil. Vathal is salted and dried. Gundruk is fermented and then dried. Smoked meat is dried by heat and kept by smoke.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Preserving Map of India. Here you draw a map and place twelve preserved foods from twelve regions on it.

flow.do: 1. Beside each food, your child writes the hurdle. 2. Ask where on the map most of the dried foods are, and where the smoked and fermented ones are. 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Look at where the sun-dried foods are, and where the smoked and fermented ones are. What is the weather like in those places? Why might that matter?
flow.kid: Write each hurdle on the map. Where are the sun-dried foods? Where are the smoked ones? Say why you think so.

ask.q: Why do people in Nagaland and Sikkim smoke and ferment food more than they sun-dry it?
good: It rains a lot there, and food does not dry well in damp air.

ask.q: Why are so many of these foods made from mango, fish or winter vegetables?
good: Those foods come in one season only, so people keep them for the rest of the year.

flow.context: In this step of the Preserving Map of India you write how each food is kept. You look for a pattern between the method and the weather.

flow.do: 1. Your child asks an older person about two foods their own family preserved. 2. They ask how each was made, in which month, and what rules had to be followed. 3. They add the two foods to the map.
flow.say: Ask what our family used to preserve, in which month, and what the rules were. Then work out which hurdle each rule was protecting.
flow.kid: Ask an older person: what did our family preserve? In which month? What were the rules? Add two foods to your map.
flow.parent: Rules such as 'dry spoon only', 'sun the jar first' and 'no wet hands' all keep water out. If no elder is available, your child can add two preserved foods from your own kitchen.

check.q: Vathal and vadam are made in March and April in Tamil Nadu. Why in those months?
options: Hot sun and dry air dry food fast
Microbes sleep in March and April
Rice is cheapest then
check.why: Drying needs hot sun and dry air. In the rainy months the pieces would stay damp and grow mould before they dried. Microbes are active all year.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Preserving Map of India. Here you ask an older person about your own family's preserved foods and add them to the map.

activities.title: Thirty Plants: what do my gut microbes get to eat?
activities.context: In this activity you count every different plant you eat in three days. Your gut microbes feed on the fibre in plants. People who eat more kinds of plants have more kinds of gut microbes.

materials.item: a notebook page and a pencil
your own meals for three days

schedule.what: Guess how many different plants you eat in three days. Start the list with today's meals.
Add today's new plants to the list.
Add today's new plants, count the total and compare it with your guess.

activities.record: Keep one list. Write each plant's name only once. At the end, write the total and one way you could add three more plants next week.

setup.art: A plate of rice, sambar, a green vegetable and curd, with small labels pointing to rice, toor dal, drumstick, tomato, onion, tamarind and curry leaf.
setup.caption: 1. Look at one meal. Name every plant in that meal.

setup.art: A notebook page with a numbered list of plants, some ticked, and a pencil.
setup.caption: 2. Keep one list for three days. Write each plant only once.

setup.art: A child counting down the finished list with one finger.
setup.caption: 3. Count your total. Compare it with your guess.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to guess how many different plants they eat in three days. 2. Look at today's meals together. 3. Name every plant: grains, dals, vegetables, fruits, nuts, seeds, herbs and spices. 4. Write each one once.
flow.say: Your gut microbes eat the fibre in plants. How many different plants do you think you eat in three days? Let's count the ones in today's lunch.
flow.kid: Guess how many different plants you eat in three days. Now name every plant in today's meals. Write each one once.
flow.parent: Rice, wheat, ragi, each kind of dal, and each vegetable and fruit all count. So do groundnuts, coconut, mustard seed, curry leaf and coriander. Sugar, oil and white flour do not add much, because their fibre has been removed. Milk, curd, egg, fish and meat are not plants.
flow.context: This is the first step of Thirty Plants. Here you guess how many different plants you eat in three days, and start a list.

flow.do: 1. On day 2, look at the day's meals. 2. Add only the plants that are new to the list.
flow.say: Which plants did you eat today that are not yet on the list? Which meal gave you the most new ones?
flow.kid: Look at today's meals. Add only the new plants to your list.
flow.wait: Add to the list on day 2
flow.context: This is the second day of Thirty Plants, where you list every different plant you eat in three days.

flow.do: 1. On day 3, add the new plants and count the total. 2. Compare the total with the guess. 3. Ask which single dish held the most plants. 4. Ask for one way to add three new plants next week.
flow.say: How many plants in three days? Was your guess close? Which dish had the most plants in it? How could you add three more next week?
flow.kid: Count your plants. Was your guess close? Which dish had the most? How could you add three more?

ask.q: Why might more kinds of plants mean more kinds of gut microbes?
good: Different microbes feed on different kinds of fibre.
More kinds of food can feed more kinds of microbes.

flow.parent: One large study counted the plants people ate in a week. Those who ate 30 or more kinds had more kinds of gut microbes. Those who ate fewer than 10 kinds had fewer. A family eating sambar, dal, sabzi and fruit often passes 30 in a week. Do not turn the number into a rule or a worry.

check.q: Why do your gut microbes depend on the plants you eat?
options: They feed on fibre that you cannot digest
Plants bring new gut microbes every day
Plants make the gut warm
check.why: Your own enzymes do not break down most fibre, so it reaches the large intestine whole. The microbes there ferment the fibre. Most gut microbes live in you all the time and are not swallowed fresh each day.

flow.context: This is the last step of Thirty Plants. Here you count the different plants you ate in three days and compare the total with your guess.

projects.title: My Own Keeping Trial: design a test and write a report
projects.context: In this six-day project you design your own fair test of ways to keep grated carrot from spoiling. You choose the methods, run the trial and write a one-page report.

materials.item: a carrot, grated by a grown-up (or a cucumber)
small clear jars or glasses with covers
kitchen things to choose from: salt, sugar or jaggery, lemon juice or vinegar, oil, the sun, the fridge
a tablespoon, a teaspoon, labels and a pen
a sheet of paper for the report

projects.safety: A grown-up grates the carrot. This trial is for looking and smelling, not for eating. Smell by waving your hand over the jar. Pour or scrape everything into the wet waste at the end, and wash the jars with hot water and soap.

schedule.what: Choose three methods and write your plan and your guesses. Set up four jars: one plain and three treated.
Look and smell. Write what you find for each jar.
Look, smell and write.
Look, smell and write.
Look, smell and write.
Do the last check. Rank the four jars and write your report.

projects.record: Your report has five parts on one page: my question, what I did, my results table, what I found, and what I would test next. Add a drawing of the four jars on the last day.

setup.art: A child writing a plan in a notebook, with a grated carrot in a bowl and salt, sugar, a lemon and oil set out to choose from.
setup.caption: 1. Choose three ways to keep grated carrot. Write your plan.

setup.art: Four small labelled jars of grated carrot in a row: Plain, and three with the child's chosen methods.
setup.caption: 2. Set up one plain jar and three treated jars.

setup.art: A one-page report with a title, a small results table and a drawing of four jars.
setup.caption: 3. Check every day. Then write a one-page report.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to choose three methods from what they have learned. 2. For each, they decide the amount, for example 1 teaspoon of salt to 2 tablespoons of carrot. 3. They write a guess for each jar, with a reason. 4. They write what will stay the same in every jar.
flow.say: This is your own trial. Which three ways of keeping food will you test? How much of each will you use? What must stay the same?
flow.kid: Choose three ways to keep carrot. Decide how much of each to use. Write your guesses and your reasons.

ask.q: Why do you need one jar with plain carrot?
good: To compare the others with.
Without it we would not know how fast carrot spoils by itself.

flow.parent: Let the plan be theirs, even if you expect a method to fail. Remind them of the Salt Ladder: a quarter teaspoon of salt did little, so the amount matters. Good plans include a lot of salt, or enough lemon juice or vinegar to cover the carrot. Drying in the sun, sugar syrup and the fridge are good too.
flow.context: This is the first step of My Own Keeping Trial. Here you choose three ways to keep grated carrot from spoiling and write a plan.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up grates the carrot. 2. Put 2 tablespoons of carrot in each of the four jars. 3. Leave one plain. Treat the other three as planned. 4. Label and cover each jar. 5. Keep them together, unless one method is the fridge or the sun.
flow.say: Measure the same amount of carrot into every jar. Label each jar with what you added and how much.
flow.kid: Put 2 tablespoons of carrot in each jar. Leave one plain. Treat the other three. Label and cover them.
flow.context: In this step of My Own Keeping Trial you set up four jars of grated carrot: one plain and three treated in ways you chose.

flow.do: 1. Each day for four days, look at each jar through the glass. 2. Look for liquid, slime, fuzz, bubbles and a change of colour. 3. Smell by waving. 4. Write the findings in the table.
flow.say: What has changed in each jar since yesterday? Which jar changed first? Is any jar still as it was on day 1?
flow.kid: Each day, look at each jar. Look for slime, fuzz and bubbles. Smell by waving. Write it down.
flow.parent: Plain grated carrot usually turns slimy and sour-smelling within two to four days in a warm kitchen. A jar that bubbles and smells pleasantly sour, like pickle, may be fermenting and not spoiling. That is worth noting in the report.
flow.wait: Check once a day from day 2 to day 5
flow.context: This step of My Own Keeping Trial is repeated on four days. You look at and smell four jars of grated carrot.

flow.do: 1. On day 6, do the last check. 2. Rank the four jars from best kept to worst. 3. Your child writes the one-page report. 4. They read it aloud to someone in the family.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which method worked best? What would you change if you ran the trial again?
flow.kid: Rank your jars. Write your report. Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened.

ask.q: One of your methods did not work. What does that tell you?
good: Maybe the amount was too small.
Maybe that method needs another hurdle with it.

check.q: One jar of carrot gets salt, lemon juice and the fridge together. That jar keeps best. What can you say?
options: Salt is the best method
You cannot tell which one did the work
The fridge did nothing
check.why: Three things were changed at once, so the result does not show which one mattered. To find out, each method needs a jar of its own. That is why a fair test changes one thing at a time.

flow.context: This is the last step of My Own Keeping Trial. Here you rank four jars of grated carrot and write a one-page report on which method kept the carrot best.

challenges.title: The Train Tiffin: food for 33 hours with no fridge
challenges.context: This is a planning challenge about keeping food on a long journey. You plan four meals for a train journey of about 33 hours, using hurdles and no fridge.
challenges.problem: A train from Chennai to New Delhi takes about 33 hours. The coach is warm, and there is no fridge and no stove. Plan four meals and two snacks for one traveller, to be packed at home before leaving. Every meal must still be safe and good to eat when its time comes.
constraints: No fridge, no ice and no reheating.
The first meal is eaten within 4 hours of packing. The last is eaten about 30 hours after packing.
For each meal, name the hurdle or hurdles that keep it safe until it is eaten.
Use at least three different hurdles across the whole plan.
No meal may depend on cooked rice, dal or cut fruit staying plain for more than 4 hours.
materials: your notes on which hurdles keep which foods
an older person who has packed food for journeys, to ask
for the test: the ingredients for one item from your plan
general: Dry foods: thepla, khakhra, chivda, roasted chana, murukku.
Sour foods with oil: puliyodarai (tamarind rice) or lemon rice with plenty of tempering.
Idli coated in oil and chutney powder, which keeps drier than idli with wet chutney.
Whole fruit with the skin on, such as bananas and oranges.
creative: Mix rice with milk and one spoon of curd in the morning. By lunchtime the curd bacteria have made fresh curd rice.
Carry dry parts and wet parts separately, and mix them at mealtime. Sattu powder with water, or puffed rice with chopped onion, works this way.
Pack each meal in its own closed box, so opening one does not let microbes into the others.
Plan the order: the wettest and least sour food is eaten first, and the driest last.
challenges.your_turn: Now write your own plan as a table: the meal, the hour it is eaten, the foods and the hurdles. Then make one item from your plan and keep it closed at room warmth for 12 hours. Let a grown-up check it.

setup.art: A child at a table with a sheet of paper ruled into a table with columns for meal, hour, food and hurdle.
setup.caption: 1. Rule a table: meal, hour eaten, food, hurdle.

setup.art: Steel tiffin boxes open on a table showing tamarind rice, thepla, a small jar of pickle and two bananas.
setup.caption: 2. Choose foods whose hurdles will last until that hour.

setup.art: One closed steel box on a kitchen shelf with a paper note showing the time it was packed.
setup.caption: 3. Make one item. Keep it closed for 12 hours. A grown-up checks it.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask your child to list foods that would not last 30 hours in a warm coach. 3. Ask why each would spoil.
flow.say: First, what would go wrong? Which foods from our usual meals would spoil in a warm train by the next day? Why?
flow.kid: Read the problem. Which of our usual foods would spoil by the next day? Say why.

ask.q: Why would plain rice and dal spoil?
good: They are wet, warm and not sour or salty, so bacteria multiply fast.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Train Tiffin. Here you work out which everyday foods would spoil on a warm train journey of 33 hours.

flow.do: 1. Your child rules the table and fills in four meals and two snacks. 2. For each, they write the hour it is eaten and its hurdles. 3. Check the plan against the five rules.
flow.say: Plan the first meal for hour 4 and the last for hour 30. For each food, tell me which hurdle keeps it safe until then.
flow.kid: Fill in your table. Write the hour for each meal. Write the hurdle that keeps each food safe.
flow.parent: Ask an older relative how they packed food for trains. Many families have a set journey menu, and each item in it uses a hurdle. A food in the plan may have no hurdle. Ask your child to move that food to the first meal, or replace it.
flow.context: In this step of the Train Tiffin you plan four meals and two snacks for a long journey. You name the hurdle that keeps each one safe.

flow.do: 1. Choose one item from the plan and make it together. 2. Pack it in a closed box and write the time. 3. Leave it at room warmth for 12 hours. 4. A grown-up looks at it and smells it, and decides whether to taste it.
flow.say: Now we test one part of your plan. After 12 hours, we look and smell. I will decide whether it is safe to taste.
flow.kid: Make one item from your plan. Pack it and write the time. After 12 hours, a grown-up checks it.
flow.parent: A grown-up decides about tasting. If the food smells or looks different from when it was packed, do not taste it. Treat that as a useful result.

check.q: Which of these is the safest choice for the last meal of a 33-hour train journey?
options: Plain rice with dal
Thepla with pickle
Cut papaya
check.why: Thepla is fairly dry and pickle is salty and sour, so both keep. Plain rice with dal is wet and has no hurdle, and cut fruit has lost the protection of its skin.

flow.wait: Leave the packed item for 12 hours
flow.context: This is the last step of the Train Tiffin. Here you make one item from your journey plan and check how it keeps for 12 hours without a fridge.

challenges.title: The Fly-Proof Dryer: dry faster than an open plate
challenges.context: This is a design challenge about drying food. In Sun-Dried Tomato, slices dried slowly on a plate under a cloth. Now you build a dryer that dries faster than an open plate and keeps flies and dust off.
challenges.problem: Food dried on an open plate dries slowly, and flies and dust can reach it. Build a dryer from things at home. It must dry a wet cloth faster than an open plate does, and no fly may get in. The wet cloth stands in for slices of food.
constraints: Use only things already at home.
Air must be able to pass through the dryer.
No fly may be able to land on the cloth inside.
The cloth inside must not touch the floor.
Test the dryer and an open plate side by side, in the same place, for the same time.
materials: a cardboard box or a shoe box
thin cotton cloth, an old net bag or a net food cover
black paper or a black cloth, and kitchen foil
sticks, skewers or a wire cooling rack
two pieces cut from one old cotton cloth, each about 10 centimetres square
a teaspoon, water, a plate, and a hanger balance or a kitchen scale
general: Line the bottom with black paper, which takes in sunlight and warms up.
Raise the food on a rack, so air reaches it from below as well.
Cover the top with net or thin cloth, so air passes and flies do not.
Tilt the dryer to face the sun.
creative: Cut holes low on one side and high on the other. Warm air rises and leaves at the top, and pulls fresh air in below.
Line a flap with foil to throw extra sunlight in.
Hang the pieces from threads, so both sides dry at once.
With no sunny spot, design for moving air and stand the dryer under a fan.
challenges.your_turn: Now build your own dryer and test it against an open plate. Draw your design, mark where the air goes in and out, and write which change made the biggest difference.

setup.art: A cardboard box with black paper inside, a wire rack across the middle and a net cover on top, standing on a sunny window sill.
setup.caption: 1. Build a dryer that lets air through and keeps flies out.

setup.art: Two identical small squares of cloth, each being wetted with two teaspoons of water.
setup.caption: 2. Wet two equal pieces of cloth with 2 teaspoons of water each.

setup.art: A hanger balance with one cloth square in each paper cup, tilted so one side hangs lower.
setup.caption: 3. After one hour, hang both on a balance. The heavier one is still wetter.

flow.do: 1. Read the problem together. 2. Ask your child what makes wet clothes dry fast on a washing line. 3. Write their list.
flow.say: On a washing line, when do clothes dry fastest? What does that tell you about what a dryer needs?
flow.kid: Read the problem. When do wet clothes dry fastest? Write your list.

ask.q: What makes wet clothes dry fastest?
good: Sun or warmth.
Wind or moving air.
Being spread out, not bunched up.
Dry air, not damp air.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Fly-Proof Dryer. Here you work out what makes things dry fast before you design a dryer.

flow.do: 1. Your child draws a design and marks where the air goes in and out. 2. Build it together from the box, the net and the rack. 3. Check it against the five rules.
flow.say: Draw your design first. Show me where the air gets in and where it gets out. Then we build it.
flow.kid: Draw your design. Mark where air goes in and out. Then build it. Check the five rules.
flow.parent: A grown-up does any cutting of cardboard. Do not correct the design before the test. The test will show what to change.
flow.context: Here you design and build the Fly-Proof Dryer from a box, a net and a rack.

flow.do: 1. Wet both cloth squares with 2 teaspoons of water each. 2. Put one inside the dryer and one on an open plate beside it. 3. After one hour, hang one in each cup of the hanger balance. 4. The side that hangs lower holds more water. 5. Change one thing in the design and test again.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why it happened. Which cloth is lighter now? What one thing will you change?
flow.kid: Wet both cloths. Put one in the dryer and one on a plate. After one hour, compare them on the balance.
flow.parent: If the open plate wins, that is a real result. A cover slows the air. Ask your child how to get more air through without letting flies in.

check.q: A dryer has a solid lid and no holes. The cloth inside stays wet. What is the most likely reason?
options: The box is too warm
The damp air inside has nowhere to go
The cloth is the wrong colour
check.why: Water leaves the cloth into the air around it. In a closed box that air soon holds all the water it can. A dryer needs air to flow through and carry the water away. Warmth helps drying.

flow.wait: Leave both cloths for one hour
flow.context: This is the last step of the Fly-Proof Dryer. Here you test your dryer against an open plate, using two equal pieces of wet cloth.

worksheets.title: Why food spoils and how we keep it

items.p: What makes food spoil?
opts: The food being kept in the dark
items.why: Bacteria, yeasts and moulds eat the food and multiply. Air alone does not spoil food, and food does not go bad just by being old: dry rice keeps for years.

items.p: Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are all ____: living beings too small to see.
items.why: Microbe is the word for any living being too small to see without a microscope.

items.p: Sort these foods by what keeps them.
items.why: Papad and milk powder have had their water removed. In honey and pickle brine, sugar or salt holds the water. Frozen peas and milk in the fridge are kept by cold.

items.p: The pinch of salt we add to dal for taste keeps the dal from spoiling.
items.why: False. In the Salt Ladder, a quarter teaspoon of salt in 100 ml did not stop the dal water from spoiling. Salt preserves only in large amounts.

items.p: Match each way of keeping food to what it does to microbes.
pairs: Holds the water so they get none
items.why: Each method takes away one thing microbes need, or kills them. Drying and salt take away free water, cold takes away warmth, oil takes away air, and boiling kills.

items.p: Thick jaggery syrup has more sugar than thin jaggery water. Why does the thick syrup keep better?
opts: Sugar is a poison for yeasts
items.why: Sugar holds on to water. In thick syrup almost no water is free, so yeasts lose water and stop growing. Sugar does not poison them: thin sugar water is their food.

items.p: Put these foods in order, from the one that spoils fastest on a shelf to the one that keeps longest.
items.why: Cooked dal is wet and warm and spoils in a day. Bread has free water and grows mould in about a week. Jam is held by sugar for weeks. Dry rice keeps for a year or more.

items.p: Freezing kills all the microbes in food.
items.why: False. Freezing stops microbes from growing, because there is no liquid water. Most are still alive, and grow again when the food warms up.

items.p: Which of these changes is caused by microbes?
items.why: Green fuzz is a mould growing. A cut apple browns by reacting with air, and a biscuit softens by taking in water. Honey turns grainy as sugar forms crystals.

items.p: Curd bacteria turn milk sugar into an ____, which makes curd sour.
items.why: The acid is lactic acid. The acid sets the milk and makes the curd sour. Most other microbes grow poorly in that acid.

items.p: Milk powder keeps for a year. Explain what changes once water is stirred in.
items.a: Milk powder is dry, so the microbes on the powder have too little water to grow. Stirring in water gives them free water again. Now it is like fresh milk and will spoil in about a day unless it is kept cold.
items.why: A strong answer says that the microbes were there all along, waiting, and that water is what lets them grow.

items.p: Explain why a wet spoon can spoil a jar of pickle.
items.a: Pickle keeps because the salt holds the water and the oil keeps air out. A wet spoon brings in fresh water that the salt has not yet held. Mould spores can grow in that water, most of all on pieces that stick out above the oil.
items.why: A strong answer names the hurdle that the water weakens. It also says that a perfectly clean spoon can still do this.

items.p: Draw a jar of mango pickle. Label four hurdles that keep the pickle from spoiling.
items.a: A jar with mango pieces fully under a layer of oil. Labels: a lot of salt, sour mango, mustard and chilli, and oil that keeps air out.
items.why: A strong drawing shows every piece below the oil, and each label says what the microbes are missing.
items.art: A blank outline of a tall pickle jar with a lid.

items.p: A lemon has grown blue-green mould. Is the lemon spoiled?

views.says: Yes. We cannot eat that lemon now. The mould may have left toxins in the lemon, and the lemon is wasted.
The lemon is my food and my home. I am eating and growing, as every living being does. Nothing has gone wrong.
In the kitchen that lemon is spoiled. In my compost heap the same mould is the first step in turning the lemon into soil.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. The cook is right that the lemon is unsafe for people. The mould is doing what every living being does, which is to eat and grow. The gardener points out that where the lemon is changes what we call it.
items.why: Each view is true from where it stands. A strong answer keeps two things apart: whether the lemon is safe for us to eat, and whether something has gone wrong in nature.

items.p: A sealed tin of food has swollen ends. What should be done with the tin?
opts: Open it and smell the food
Boil the food and eat it
items.why: Gas from bacteria that grow without air has swollen the tin. They can make a deadly toxin that tasting or boiling at home will not make safe.

items.p: With no salt or a quarter teaspoon, dal water spoiled. With 2 teaspoons it kept. What does this show?
opts: Any amount of salt stops spoiling
Salt works only in large amounts
Salt has no effect on microbes
items.why: A small amount of salt made no difference, and a large amount stopped the spoiling. So salt preserves only above a certain strength.

items.p: Honey is one-sixth water. Bread is over one-third water. Why does only the bread go mouldy?
opts: No spores ever land on honey
items.why: What matters is free water. In honey the sugar holds nearly all the water. In bread much of the water is free for moulds to use.

items.p: Why do moulds not grow under the oil in a pickle jar?
opts: Oil is too cold for them
Moulds need air, and oil keeps air out
items.why: Moulds must have air. The oil keeps air away from the pickle. Pieces that stick out above the oil can grow mould.

items.p: No living microbes are left on dried food.
items.why: False. Drying stops microbes from growing but does not kill them all. Many wait as spores, and grow if the food gets damp.

items.p: Curd keeps longer than the milk it was made from.
items.why: True. The curd bacteria fill the milk with acid, and most other microbes grow poorly in that acid.

items.p: Sort these into spoiled, fermented, or only changed without microbes.
items.why: Frothy dal and slimy spinach were changed by microbes nobody chose. Idli batter and curd were set to ferment on purpose. A cut apple reacts with air, and a biscuit takes in water from the air.

items.p: Three of these keep food by leaving too little free water. Which is the odd one out?
items.why: Drying removes water, and salt and sugar hold it. The fridge leaves the water where it is and works by slowing microbes with cold.

items.p: A brine needs 12 grams of salt in every 100 ml. How many grams are needed for 500 ml?
items.why: 500 ml is 5 lots of 100 ml. 5 times 12 grams is 60 grams.

items.p: Put the steps of a fair Salt Ladder test in order.
items: Check every glass twice a day and write what you see
Add a different amount of salt to each glass
Make one pot of dal water
Leave all the glasses open for the same time, then cover them
Pour the same amount into each glass
a: Make one pot of dal water
Pour the same amount into each glass
Add a different amount of salt to each glass
Leave all the glasses open for the same time, then cover them
Check every glass twice a day and write what you see
items.why: Everything is kept the same except the salt: one pot, equal amounts, equal time in the air. Then the checks show what the salt alone did.

items.p: Thick jaggery syrup did not ferment. How could you show that it was only short of water?
items.a: Take a spoon of the same thick syrup and stir it into water. If it now ferments, nothing in the syrup was stopping the yeasts. The only thing added was water.
items.why: A strong answer changes one thing only, the water, and says what result would support the idea.

items.p: Dried fish is salted as well as dried. Give one reason why two hurdles are better than one.
items.a: If the fish takes in a little water from damp air, the salt still holds that water. A microbe that can stand dryness may not stand salt. So when one hurdle weakens, the other still works.
items.why: A strong answer says what could go wrong with one hurdle alone, and how the second covers for it.

items.p: Tomato slices sealed in a clean jar spoiled. Slices dried in open air did not. Explain why.
items.a: Microbes were already on the tomato skin and the knife, so they were in the jar too. The sealed slices kept all their water, and the microbes grew. The dried slices lost most of their water, so the microbes on them were unable to grow.
items.why: A strong answer says the microbes were on both sets from the start, and that water made the difference.

items.p: Should food made in factories have added preservatives?

views.says: A small, tested amount of preservative stops food poisoning and stops food being wasted. That is a good trade.
Salt, sour fruit, oil and sunshine have kept food in this family for a hundred years. I see no need for numbers on a label.
Both of you add something to keep food. A lot of salt or sugar also harms health. The question is how much of each we eat.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that every preserved food uses hurdles, and salt and sugar are preservatives too. Another is that food poisoning and wasted food are real harms.
items.why: This is a real trade-off. A strong answer weighs a harm on each side. It does not treat either 'natural' or 'tested' as the end of the matter.

items.p: Label this thermometer with what most microbes do at minus 18, 4, 30 and 72 degrees Celsius.
a: Minus 18 degrees (freezer): they stop growing but most stay alive
items.why: Cold slows and then stops growth without killing. Kitchen warmth is where spoiling microbes grow fastest. Strong heat kills most of them.
items.art: A tall thermometer with four blank label lines at minus 18, 4, 30 and 72 degrees Celsius.

items.p: Water moving out of a microbe's cell into salty water is called ____.
items.why: In osmosis, water passes through the cell's thin skin. The water moves towards the side with more salt or sugar dissolved.

items.p: Cooked rice sat out all day and was then fried until very hot. Is the rice safe now?
opts: Not always: some toxins survive heat
Yes, as long as it smells fine
items.why: Frying kills the bacteria, but some bacteria leave toxins in the rice that heat does not destroy. Smell is no guide, because this rice can smell normal.

items.p: Hot countries use more spices. Does this prove that spices are used to stop food spoiling?
opts: No, other reasons could explain the pattern
items.why: Two things going together does not show that one causes the other. Hot countries also grow more spice plants, for example. A later study found that spice use does not match the risk of illness from food.

items.p: A test compares salt, lemon juice and drying as ways to keep carrot. Which jar is still needed?
opts: A jar with all three together
items.why: Without a plain jar, there is nothing to compare with. Nobody would know how fast the carrot spoils when nothing is done to it.

items.p: Which finding shows that air alone does not spoil food?
opts: Sealed tins with no air inside spoiled
Dry rice kept for a year
items.why: If air were the cause, a tin with no air could never spoil. Bacteria that survived weak heating spoiled such tins from inside.

items.p: If food looks and smells normal, it is always safe to eat.
items.why: False. Some harmful bacteria reach dangerous numbers, or leave toxins, without changing the look or smell of the food.

items.p: The fuzzy patch you see is the whole of a mould on bread.
items.why: False. The fuzz is the part that makes spores. Fine threads run deep into the bread, further than the patch you can see.

items.p: Match each preserved thing to what kept it.
items.why: The same hurdles that keep food keep anything microbes would eat: salt and dryness, cold, sugar, and heating in a sealed pack.

items.p: Six tomato slices weigh 80 grams fresh and 8 grams when dried. How many grams of water left them?
items.why: 80 grams minus 8 grams is 72 grams. So 72 of the 80 grams, or nine-tenths, was water that left.

items.p: Some bacteria double every 30 minutes. In 2 hours, one bacterium becomes ____ bacteria.
items.why: Two hours is four lots of 30 minutes. 1 doubles to 2, then 4, then 8, then 16.

items.p: Milk keeps for days at 4 degrees but spoils in a day at 30 degrees. Use doubling to explain why.
items.a: At 30 degrees bacteria may double every half hour, so a few become millions in a few hours. At 4 degrees they double only once in many hours, so their numbers stay low for days. The fridge does not kill them. It makes each doubling slow.
items.why: A strong answer says that the same doubling happens in both places. Only the time for each doubling is different.

items.p: Design a fair test to find how much sugar stops jaggery water from fermenting.
items.a: Make a ladder of glasses with the same water and more jaggery in each. For example, use 1, 2, 4, 6 and 8 tablespoons in 8 tablespoons of water. Add the same pinch of atta to each and keep them together. Check each day and note the first day each one bubbles. The answer lies between the last glass that ferments and the first that does not.
items.why: A strong answer has several steps of sugar and keeps everything else the same. It says how the result will be read.

items.p: Many people cut the mould off bread and eat the rest. What would you tell them, and why?
items.a: I would tell them to throw the whole slice away. The fuzz is only the part of the mould that makes spores. Threads have already grown through the soft bread, and some moulds leave toxins there.
items.why: A strong answer gives the reason, the hidden threads, and does not only repeat the rule.

items.p: In one study, 36 adults ate fermented foods for ten weeks and gained gut microbes. Give two reasons for caution.
items.a: 36 people is a small number. Ten weeks is short, and nobody knows whether the change lasts. The people were all adults, so children might differ. Other things in their meals may have changed too.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different reasons, such as the size of the study, its length, or who took part.

items.p: A packet of food is one day past its 'best before' date. Eat it or throw it away?

views.says: 'Best before' is a promise that the food is at its best until that day. Dry foods like biscuits and dal are still safe after it.
For milk, meat and cooked food, dates matter. Harmful microbes can be there with no smell, and a day's saving is not worth an illness.

views.who: Someone who works to cut food waste
views.says: About one-third of all food is lost or wasted. Look, smell and think about what kind of food it is before you throw it away.

items.ask: Which view do you agree with most? Give a reason from what you have learned. Then answer one of the other views.
items.a: Any view with a reason from the unit. One reason is that dry foods have a strong hurdle and change slowly. Another is that wet foods can be unsafe with no sign.
items.why: A strong answer says that the right choice depends on the kind of food and its hurdles. It uses one example of each.

items.p: Draw a yeast cell in thin jaggery water and one in thick syrup. Show with arrows how water moves.
items.a: In thin jaggery water the cell is plump, and arrows show water moving in. In thick syrup the cell is shrunken, and arrows show water moving out of the cell into the syrup.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the direction of the water and the change in the cell's size. It labels which side has more sugar.
items.art: Two blank glasses side by side, one labelled thin and one labelled thick.

quiz.p: Which three kinds of microbes most often spoil food?
quiz.why: Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are the microbes that eat food and multiply there. Flies and ants are animals we can see, and they are not what makes dal froth or bread grow fuzz.

quiz.p: Which of these do spoiling microbes need in order to grow?
quiz.why: Microbes can grow only where there is water they can take in. Salt and cold both hold them back, and light makes little difference.

opts: It adds sunlight to the food
It leaves too little water for microbes
quiz.why: Dried food has too little free water for microbes to grow. Many microbes are still on the food, waiting. That is why dried food must stay dry.

quiz.p: Why does pickle have to be very salty?
opts: Salt works only in large amounts
quiz.why: A little salt leaves plenty of free water for microbes. Only a lot of salt holds enough of the water to stop them.

quiz.p: What does a fridge do to most microbes in food?
quiz.why: Cold slows the growth of microbes. They are still alive, so food from the fridge spoils once it is left warm.

quiz.p: Jam and murabba keep for months because they are:
quiz.why: At that strength the sugar holds the water, so microbes get almost none. Fruit alone spoils quickly, and glass does nothing without the sugar.

quiz.p: Idli batter has risen overnight and smells a little sour. The batter is:
quiz.why: Bacteria and yeasts that we wanted have made gas and acid in the batter. That is fermentation. Spoiling is the work of microbes nobody chose.

quiz.p: A crisp biscuit left out overnight now bends. What happened to the biscuit?
opts: Microbes ate part of the biscuit
It took in water from the air
quiz.why: Dry food takes in water vapour from damp air. No microbes are needed for that, though mould can follow if the biscuit stays damp.

quiz.p: Why does curd keep better than milk?
quiz.why: Curd is full of living bacteria. The acid they made holds back most other microbes.

quiz.p: What do your gut microbes eat that your own body is unable to digest?
quiz.why: Your enzymes do not break down most fibre, so it reaches the large intestine. Gut microbes ferment the fibre, and what they make feeds your gut wall.

quiz.p: In a fair test of how much salt keeps food, what is the one thing that changes?
quiz.why: Only the amount of salt changes. If the food, the glass or the place also changed, nobody could tell which one caused the result.

quiz.p: What are scientists still unsure of about curd and other fermented foods?
opts: Whether their bacteria settle in the gut
Whether they are safe to eat
quiz.why: Fermented foods are safe and do hold living bacteria. What is still being tested is whether those bacteria stay in the gut and change a person's health.

applications: Long-life milk in cartons is heated to about 140 degrees Celsius for a few seconds and packed with no microbes. It keeps for months without a fridge until it is opened.
Farmers dry rice, wheat and groundnuts well before storing them. Damp grain grows moulds, and some of those moulds make toxins.
Cold stores in Himachal Pradesh, Uttar Pradesh and West Bengal keep apples and potatoes for many months after the harvest.
Fishing families along the coasts of Kerala, Tamil Nadu, Gujarat and Odisha salt and dry part of the catch. This is the part that cannot be sold fresh.
Small sachets of silica gel are packed with snacks, shoes and medicines. They take water out of the air inside, so the contents stay dry.
Vaccines are carried to villages in cold boxes. Cold slows the changes that would spoil them, as it does for food.
Seed banks keep dried seeds at minus 18 degrees Celsius. Dry and cold together let seeds wait alive for many decades.
Food for astronauts and for soldiers on mountains is dried, or heated in sealed pouches. It keeps for a year or more without a fridge.

open_questions.q: Do the living bacteria in fermented foods settle in our gut, and does that change our health?
open_questions.why_open: The studies so far are small and short. In some people swallowed bacteria settle, and in others they pass straight through, and nobody yet knows why.

open_questions.q: How long can a dried or frozen microbe stay alive?
open_questions.why_open: Bacteria have been grown from ice and from salt crystals that are very old. Some scientists think those bacteria got in later, and the oldest claims are disputed.

open_questions.q: How does a microbe sense that water is running short, and decide to form a spore?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know some of the signals inside the cell. They do not know the whole chain from sensing dryness to making a spore.

open_questions.q: Do bacteria on food signal to each other before they spoil the food?
open_questions.why_open: Many bacteria release chemical signals, and act differently once they are crowded. Whether these signals set off spoiling in real foods is still being studied.

open_questions.q: Can a full, tasty diet be kept fresh for a journey of several years, such as a journey to Mars?
open_questions.why_open: Packed food stays safe for years, but vitamins and taste slowly fade. Nobody has yet shown a food system that keeps people well fed for that long.

jokes.a: It had millions of sour bodyguards.

maths.problem: In the Salt Ladder, the glass with 2 teaspoons of salt in 100 ml held about 12 grams of salt. How much salt makes 500 ml of brine of the same strength? How many teaspoons is that?
maths.explain: 500 ml is 5 lots of 100 ml. 5 times 12 grams is 60 grams. Each teaspoon is about 6 grams, and 60 divided by 6 is 10.
maths.context: This is about the Salt Ladder. In it, five glasses of dal water get different amounts of salt, and you watch which ones spoil.
maths.why_maths: A recipe for brine must work for any size of jar. Keeping the same share of salt to water does that.

maths.problem: These are made-up results from a Salt Ladder. Each bar shows the check at which a glass first spoiled, and 7 means it never spoiled. What is the smallest amount of salt that kept the dal water? Between which two amounts does 'spoils' change to 'keeps'?
maths.answer: 2 teaspoons kept it. The change comes between 1 and 2 teaspoons.
maths.explain: The bars for 2 and 4 teaspoons both reach 7, so those glasses never spoiled. The bar for 1 teaspoon stops at 5, so that glass spoiled late. So the change lies between 1 and 2 teaspoons in 100 ml.
maths.context: This is about the Salt Ladder. In it, five glasses of dal water get different amounts of salt, and you watch which ones spoil.

chart.title: Made-up example: the check at which each glass first spoiled
chart.y: Number of the check (7 means never)

maths.why_maths: A chart of the whole ladder shows where the change happens. One glass alone could not show that.

maths.problem: In Sun-Dried Tomato, six slices weighed 80 grams fresh and 8 grams after drying. What percentage of the fresh weight was water that left?
maths.explain: The water that left weighed 80 minus 8, which is 72 grams. 72 out of 80 is the same as 9 out of 10, or 90 out of 100.
maths.context: This is about Sun-Dried Tomato, where you weigh tomato slices before and after drying them in the sun. These weights are made up.
maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare your tomato with someone else's, even if their slices were bigger.

maths.problem: Suppose the bacteria in warm dal double every 30 minutes. There are 100 at lunch. How many are there 4 hours later? In the fridge, suppose they double every 12 hours. How many are there after the same 4 hours?
maths.answer: 25,600 in the warm dal. Still about 100 in the fridge.
maths.explain: 4 hours is 8 lots of 30 minutes, so the number doubles 8 times: 200, 400, 800, 1,600, 3,200, 6,400, 12,800, 25,600. In the fridge, 4 hours is less than one doubling time, so the number has hardly changed.
maths.context: This is about why warm food spoils fast and cold food keeps. Bacteria multiply by splitting in two.
maths.why_maths: Doubling grows much faster than people expect. Working it out shows why a few hours on the counter matter so much.

maths.problem: 100 grams of honey hold about 17 grams of water. 100 grams of bread hold about 38 grams of water. Which holds more water? Which one grows mould? What does this tell you about total water and free water?
maths.answer: Bread holds more than twice as much water, and bread grows mould. So free water matters, and the total amount of water does not.
maths.explain: 38 is more than twice 17. In honey, sugar holds nearly all of the 17 grams. In bread, much of the 38 grams is free. So counting water alone does not tell you whether a food will keep.
maths.context: This follows Thick or Thin, where thin jaggery water fermented and thick jaggery syrup did not.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two numbers shows that the amount of water alone does not explain the result. Another idea is needed.

maths.problem: In Thick or Thin, the thin glass has 1 tablespoon of jaggery to 8 of water. The thick glass has 8 tablespoons of jaggery to 3 of water. What fraction of each mixture is jaggery? In which glass is more than half the mixture jaggery?
maths.answer: Thin: 1 ninth. Thick: 8 elevenths. Only the thick glass is more than half jaggery.
maths.explain: The thin glass has 1 + 8 = 9 spoons in all, and 1 of them is jaggery. The thick glass has 8 + 3 = 11 spoons in all, and 8 of them are jaggery. Half of 11 is 5 and a half, and 8 is more than that.
maths.context: This is about Thick or Thin, where you mix jaggery and water at three strengths and watch which ones ferment.
maths.why_maths: A fraction says how strong a mixture is, whatever the size of the glass. It lets you compare your syrup with jam or honey.

odd: Papad, milk powder and raisins are kept by dryness, but frozen peas are kept by cold.
Curd, idli batter and gundruk are fermented on purpose, but mouldy bread is spoiled.
The apple, the biscuit and the honey changed without microbes, but frothy dal was changed by bacteria.
Salt, sugar and drying leave too little free water, but vinegar works by being sour.
Bacteria, yeasts and moulds are living microbes, but salt is a mineral.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out why heating and sealing keeps food? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: In the 1790s, armies and ships needed food that would keep for months. Nicolas Appert, a cook and sweet-maker in Paris, tried for many years to find a way. He packed soups, peas and fruit into glass bottles, corked them tightly and heated them in boiling water. The food kept. In 1810 the French government paid him 12,000 francs, on the condition that he made his method public. Appert did not know why it worked. The chemist Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac tested the bottles. He is said to have argued that air spoils food. He thought the bottled food kept because no air was left to act on it. Many scientists accepted this for years. In the 1860s Louis Pasteur showed that living microbes, carried on dust in the air, do the spoiling. The heat had killed the microbes in the bottle, and the cork kept new ones out. In the 1890s Samuel Prescott and William Underwood, in the United States, opened swollen tins of clams and corn. No air had got in, yet the food had spoiled. They found living bacteria inside, whose spores had survived too little heating.
how_we_found_out.who: Nicolas Appert, a cook in Paris. Joseph Louis Gay-Lussac and Louis Pasteur, French chemists. Samuel Prescott and William Underwood in the United States.
how_we_found_out.when: Appert published his method in 1810. Pasteur's work was in the 1860s. Prescott and Underwood worked on tins from 1895 to 1898.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That air itself spoils food, and that food keeps when the air is taken away. Pasteur showed that microbes do the spoiling. Prescott and Underwood found food spoiled by bacteria inside tins that no air had entered.

roots.context: We have tested how salt and sugar stop microbes, and learned how people keep food. Now we ask what this tells us about water, about life and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In Thick or Thin, the thin jaggery water fermented and the thick jaggery syrup did not. Both glasses held the same jaggery and the same pinch of atta, which carries wild yeasts. In the thick syrup, the sugar holds on to the water, so the yeasts can take almost none. So a food can feel wet to us and still be too dry for a microbe.
deep_truth.habit: We call a food wet or dry by how it feels to our fingers. We treat wetness as one fact about the food. For a living cell, what matters is how much of the water is free to take. Honey is about one-sixth water and keeps for years. Bread feels dry and grows mould in a week.
deep_truth.evidence: In Thick or Thin, the thick syrup stays unchanged for five days. When a spoon of that same syrup is stirred into water, it ferments within a few days. In the Salt Ladder, the glass with 4 teaspoons of salt is still a liquid. Yet it stays clear while the unsalted glass spoils. If your own results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: Your cells need free water too. After very salty food you feel thirsty, because the salt in your blood is holding water that your cells need.
three.what_is_life: A living being can wait. A dried yeast cell, or a mould spore on a papad, does nothing we can see for months. Give them water, and they grow again.
three.what_is_this_world: Water is in most places on Earth, but living beings can use it only where it is free. A salt pan, a jar of honey and a desert are each dry in their own way.

roots.thread: Every living being, from a yeast cell to you, is mostly water and must take in free water to grow. All life shares this need, because all life descends from the same first cells, who lived in water. So one rule explains many kitchens. Avakaya in Andhra Pradesh, dried fish in Kerala and murabba in Uttar Pradesh all keep free water from microbes. People who never met each other found the same answer. They were all dealing with the same living beings and the same need.

teachings.teaching: From food all beings are born. By food they live, and into food they pass when they die.
teachings.link: A mango that we do not eat is eaten by moulds and bacteria. The mango returns to the soil as food for plants. In this unit's science too, everything alive is food for someone.

teachings.link: Preserving slows spoiling but never ends it. Honey keeps for years, yet spoils once water gets in. A cook who keeps food well is working carefully with that fact.

science.text: All known life needs liquid water to grow. No living being has been found growing where the measure of free water is below about 0.6.
Whether the living bacteria in fermented foods settle in a person's gut for long is still being tested.
Nobody knows how long a dried or frozen microbe can stay alive. Reports of bacteria revived after millions of years are disputed.

other_view.who: Doctors and scientists who work on food safety
other_view.view: They would say that it is too gentle to talk about microbes as neighbours who share our food. Unsafe food makes about 600 million people ill every year, and small children suffer most. For a family with little to eat, a spoiled meal is a real loss. In their view, the first duty is to keep microbes out of food, and wonder comes second.

practice.title: A raisin takes back water
practice.say: Hold one raisin in your palm. Look at the wrinkles. A raisin is a grape that has lost most of its water to the sun and the air. Now put the raisin on your tongue, and do not chew. Breathe slowly ten times. Feel the raisin soften as it takes water from your mouth. Now chew slowly. The sweetness you taste is the sugar that kept microbes away.
practice.kid: Hold one raisin. Look at the wrinkles. Put it on your tongue. Do not chew. Breathe slowly ten times. Feel the raisin get softer. It is taking water from your mouth. Now chew slowly and taste the sugar.

ask: Honey feels wet to you, and it is too dry for a yeast. So is honey wet or dry?
A dried yeast cell can wait for years and then grow. Is the cell alive while waiting? How could you find out?
Families all over India worked out how to keep food long before anyone had seen a microbe. How did they know what works?

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game and challenge was reasoned through step by step for a family in a city flat. None has yet been tried at home. So the timings and results below are expected, not measured. The Salt Ladder (core) needs dal, salt and five clear glasses. In a warm kitchen, glasses A and B should turn cloudy and sour within one to two days. They hold no salt and a quarter teaspoon. Glasses D and E, with 2 and 4 teaspoons, should stay as they were. Glass C, with 1 teaspoon, is the uncertain one. In a cool room everything is slower, and the steps say to go on for two more days. Very salty dal water can look slightly different from the start. So each glass is compared with how that same glass looked on day 1. Thick or Thin (core) needs about 200 grams of jaggery or sugar and a pinch of atta. The thin glass should bubble within two to three days in warm weather. Jaggery differs from block to block, so the day may vary. A white skin or mould counts as a change too. Nothing from either test is tasted. Sun-Dried Tomato needs three sunny days or a ceiling fan. In the monsoon the open slices may grow mould before they dry, and the step says to record that. The hanger balance is good to about 5 grams. In the Snap Test, the biscuit on the open plate depends on the weather. The biscuit beside the damp cloth softens in any season. My Own Keeping Trial is the child's own design. Some methods will fail, and that is part of the project. The Train Tiffin ends with a grown-up deciding whether a packed item is safe to taste. No part needs a garden.
